NEW DELHI: The Centre on Thursday told the Supreme Court that it is considering constituting a committee to revisit the University Grants Commission 's (UGC) notified rules introduced to prevent caste discrimination in educational institutions, Bar and Bench reported.Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi that the Centre is examining the issue to address students' concerns and ensure that no section feels dissatisfied or apprehensive."The government has taken a decision that every student should be taken care of. Nobody should have any apprehension. Nobody should feel dissatisfied. We are also considering the interests of the younger generation. The government is contemplating appointing a committee," SG Mehta told the apex court.This comes as the apex court was hearing a batch of petitions challenging the UGC regulations.The 2026 regulations had already been kept in abeyance by the top court on January 29.At the time, the court said the provisions were "prima facie vague" and could have "very sweeping consequences", warning that they could potentially divide society and have a "dangerous impact".The court had also asked the Centre and the UGC to respond to three petitions challenging the new framework."In exercise of our powers under Article 142 of the Constitution, we further direct that the University Grants Commission (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulations, 2012, will continue to operate and remain in force till further orders," it had said.The regulations had faced opposition in several places, with student groups and other organisations calling for their immediate withdrawal.
Article Summary: The Centre told the Supreme Court that it is considering constituting a committee to revisit the University Grants Commission's notified rules. The rules were introduced to prevent caste discrimination in educational institutions. The 2026 regulations had already been kept in abeyance by the top court on January 29.

Article Title: Delhi pollution worsens, AQI hits 482 as 7 stations record severe levels
Article Text:
India Gate records AQI of 399

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the main cause of pollution in Delhi? Vehicular emissions Construction activities Stubble burning Weather conditions 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

(With Agency Inputs)





NEW DELHI: Delhi's air quality remained in the severe category on Thursday morning, with the overall Air Quality Index (AQI) touching 482 at 8.01am. Several parts of the national capital continued to record high pollution levels.According to Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data, seven monitoring stations recorded AQI levels above 400, falling in the severe category.Punjabi Bagh recorded the highest AQI at 446, followed by Narela at 434, Rohini at 431, RK Puram at 416, Bawana at 412, North Campus, Delhi University, at 408 and Patparganj at 405.Several other areas reported very poor air quality. Okhla Phase-2 and India Gate both recorded an AQI of 399, followed by ITO at 397, Dwarka Sector 8 at 396, Chandni Chowk at 356 and Vasundhara Enclave at 330.Anand Vihar recorded an AQI of 293, while the IMD Lodhi Road station reported 268. Both stations fell in the poor category.Amid the deterioration in Delhi's air quality, Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav said on Tuesday that the Centre's air quality panel was continuously monitoring meteorological conditions, including wind direction, wind speed and the movement of air. He also assured that necessary action was being taken.The worsening air quality comes despite a decline in stubble-burning incidents compared to previous years. The government has claimed that a significant portion of paddy stubble has been utilised through ex-situ management.Asked about the reduction in stubble-burning incidents in neighbouring states, including Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, Yadav said, “Yes, I have already stated that around 40 per cent of the paddy stubble has been utilised through ex-situ management this time."Responding to reporter’s question on why air quality continues to remain in the severe category despite these measures, Yadav said the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) was closely monitoring meteorological conditions and taking necessary steps based on its assessments.“CAQM is continuously monitoring meteorological conditions, including wind direction, wind speed and the movement of air. Based on these assessments, the necessary steps are being taken,” he said.Dr Saurabh Mittal, Assistant Professor in the Department of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine at AIIMS, Delhi, said, "Since AQI has increased, we are seeing patients who have prior respiratory problems, but now they are coming with increased symptoms and exacerbations, for which we need to increase their medications, like their inhaler doses have to be increased, and some patients need the addition of new medications such as oral steroids also to reduce their cough. We are also seeing patients who have previously been asymptomatic, but now, because of the increased pollution, they are developing respiratory symptoms in terms of cough, irritation of the throat, nasal irritation, and shortness of breath. So those patients also need some kind of treatment or decongestants for symptom relief... There has been an increase in people actually calling us... I would say that we anticipate that this number is probably going to increase in the next couple of weeks..."Explaining the factors contributing to the pollution, Mittal said, "It's a multifactorial problem. It's not a one-time or one-day problem. Of course, weather contributes significantly to it; as the winter weather appears, the condensation happens. Of course, vehicular emissions, construction, stubble burning - all of these things contribute to a larger extent. But individual contribution is very difficult to kind of quantify. But yes, if we reduce all of them, it's likely that we'll have some relief from the problem."
Article Summary: Delhi's air quality remained in the severe category on Thursday morning. The overall Air Quality Index (AQI) touched 482 at 8.01am. Seven monitoring stations recorded AQI levels above 400. The worsening air quality comes despite a decline in stubble-burning incidents.

Article Title: Trump’s ‘Freedom In Space’ signals new contest for Moon; India’s challenge is safeguarding strategic autonomy
Article Text:
Trump's space declaration sparks a new Moon rules contest, forcing India to balance Artemis ties and 2047 ambitions against strategic autonomy.

Competing frameworks, competing interests

India’s strategic dilemma

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: As Americans voted in the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump issued a proclamation titled “The American Declaration of Freedom in Space”, declaring that the US would lead the exploration, development, use and settlement of space.Promising a return to the Moon by 2028, a permanent American lunar presence and an eventual human mission to Mars, the proclamation links space leadership directly to economic prosperity and national security.But beneath its rhetoric of freedom and exploration lies a larger geopolitical question: who will set the rules for humanity’s expansion beyond Earth, and will space remain a global commons or become an arena of competing national interests? For India, which has its own ambitions for human spaceflight and lunar exploration, the declaration brings this question into sharper focus.Susmita Mohanty, director general of space think tank Spaceport SARABHAI, says: “Trump describes space as ‘the province of all humans’ while, almost in the same breath, declaring his intention to establish a ‘permanent presence by American citizens’. The tension between these two assertions is difficult to ignore: a domain ostensibly belonging to all humanity is simultaneously being framed as a sphere for enduring American dominance,” she said.She also questioned the assertion of American superiority, pointing to the history of international contributions to space exploration. Russia, for instance, remained indispensable to American human spaceflight for nearly nine years after the retirement of the Space Shuttle fleet in 2011, transporting US astronauts to the International Space Station until SpaceX's Crew Dragon began crewed flights in 2020.Mohanty also pointed to China’s growing capabilities. Since 2007, China has completed six lunar missions, including two sample-return missions, and is working towards landing astronauts by 2030. “Space exploration has historically been a collaborative endeavour, one that repeatedly reminds terrestrial superpowers that their dominance has its limits,” she said.The implications extend beyond the US-China lunar race. Lt Gen AK Bhatt (retd), director-general of the Indian Space Association (ISpA), believes the proclamation signals a shift towards competing frameworks for governing space activities.“There’s now a clear divide of two groups: the Artemis-led group and the ILRS-led (China-Russia) group. Space colonisation, ownership and other things that have been talked about will definitely sow the seeds for future contests and maybe confrontation,” he said.The legal question is particularly important. Article I of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty describes space as the province of all mankind, while Article III prohibits national appropriation of celestial bodies. The proclamation, however, explicitly speaks of establishing a permanent American presence and developing resources, subject to international obligations. It does not itself confer ownership of lunar territory.India’s position is complicated by its participation in multiple international frameworks. It signed the Artemis Accords in June 2023, but also signed the 1979 Moon Agreement, which it has not ratified. The two frameworks have different approaches to aspects of lunar resource governance.In Aug 2026, Nasa invited Isro to join its Moon Base programme, building on the Artemis partnership. India, meanwhile, has its own Space Vision 2047, including the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035 and a human Moon landing by 2040.For Bhatt, this calls for a wider national debate on India's positioning. “The issue is basically where India aligns its cards. Though signing of the Artemis Accords was an indicator of our inclination, there has to be an internal debate within the Indian community,” he said.He also cautioned against dismissing the proclamation as political rhetoric. “It does not matter whether we take Donald Trump seriously or not. The signature on the paper is that of the President of the United States, aligning the policy for the future.”For India, the challenge may be to work with competing space powers without being confined to their geopolitical choices, while ensuring it has a say in the rules governing the next frontier.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump issued a proclamation titled ‘The American Declaration of Freedom in Space’ The proclamation promises a return to the Moon by 2028, a permanent American lunar presence and an eventual human mission to Mars. For India, which has its own ambitions for human spaceflight and lunar exploration, the declaration brings this question into sharper focus.

Article Title: Andhra, Kerala top ease of vehicle ownership index; UP, Bihar at bottom: Report
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Tamil Nadu have emerged as the top-performing states in ease of vehicle ownership, while Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal rank at the bottom, reflecting wide disparities in procedures for transferring ownership of used vehicles.The findings are part of the Ease of Vehicle Ownership Index (EVOI) 2026, prepared by Consumer Voice and Indiatech, which assessed systems and procedures across 15 major states and Delhi, covering more than 85% of India’s organised pre-owned vehicle market.None of the states figured in the ‘high ease’ or excellent category, with Andhra Pradesh, the highest-ranked state, scoring only 5.9 on a scale of 0-10. Kerala scored 5.7, followed by Tamil Nadu and Delhi at 4.6 each. Karnataka (4.3), Gujarat (4.2), Madhya Pradesh (4.1), Maharashtra and Telangana (4.1 each) and Punjab (4) occupied the next positions.Rajasthan (4) and Haryana (3.9) were also in the lower half of the rankings, while West Bengal (2.6), Bihar (2.5) and Uttar Pradesh (2.5) brought up the rear.The report comes as India’s pre-owned vehicle market is expanding rapidly and is projected to grow from $36.4 billion in 2025 to over $73.5 billion by 2030.The market has overtaken new vehicle sales in volume. However, fragmented state-level rules, incomplete digitisation and cumbersome procedures continue to impede seamless vehicle ownership transfers.The report, which also included interviews, found that 39% of citizens reported delays in receiving their registration certificates after completing vehicle transfers, while 61.5% were unaware of the requirement for a party-pusher until they reached the respective RTO.As many as 63% could not accurately estimate the total cost of completing an ownership transfer, reflecting widespread opacity in transaction charges.Interestingly, all respondents said they relied on intermediaries or agents to complete ownership transfers because of administrative complexity.The report has called for a unified digital vehicle records system, standardised no-objection certificate procedures, real-time integration between banks and transport departments for automatic removal of hypothecation after loan repayment, and transparent, time-bound service delivery across RTOs.
Article Summary: Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Tamil Nadu have emerged as the top-performing states in ease of vehicle ownership. Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal rank at the bottom. The findings are part of the Ease of Vehicle Ownership Index (EVOI) 2026, prepared by Consumer Voice and Indiatech.

Article Title: 'Dialled wrong number, season of dharna': CJI's quip at man seeking rotation of SC-ST reserved seats
Article Text:
CJI Surya Kant

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Wednesday quipped at a petitioner to organise public protests and demonstrations while rejecting his plea seeking mandatory rotation of seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Parliament and state assemblies.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana upheld the Allahabad high court order validating Section 9(1)(c) of the Delimitation Act, 2002, which provides for the identification of reserved constituencies in areas where the proportion of SC/ST residents is comparatively high.The Supreme Court, however, said the petitioner was free to approach public representatives and persuade them to adopt the principle of rotation."You are dialling the wrong number. This is a season of dharna, protest etc. You should also do the same," Bar and Bench quoted CJI Surya Kant as saying in a lighter vein."This is also a good ground for protest," he added.During the hearing, Justice Bagchi said that in a multiparty democracy, voters are expected to make electoral choices based on political ideologies rather than caste or religious considerations."In a political democracy, there are multiple political parties having different ideologies.The voters are expected to vote for the party, not for the religion. You may like or dislike a particular political ideology. Who is representing that ideology becomes irrelevant. You vote for that ideology. So that also defeats your argument," Justice Bagchi said.The bench also distinguished between the right to vote and any claimed right to contest an election from a particular constituency. It observed that candidates belonging to the general category remain eligible to contest from constituencies that are not reserved.The petitioner, Jagdish Singh, had challenged the continued reservation of his constituency for Scheduled Castes, claiming that it had remained reserved for nearly seven decades since its creation.He argued that the absence of a rotation mechanism violated Articles 14, 15 and 19 of the Constitution and restricted voters' electoral choices by limiting the candidates they could elect to members of the SC community.He further claimed that the existing arrangement benefited a handful of political families rather than advancing the interests of the wider community.Seeking a mechanism similar to the rotational reservation provided for panchayats and municipalities under Articles 243D and 243T of the Constitution, the petitioner urged the bench to direct periodic rotation of SC/ST-reserved constituencies.Justice Bagchi, however, disagreed with the argument that candidates from the majority community would anyway get elected in constituencies with a high SC population, making reservation unnecessary."That proceeds on the idea that a majority community will vote on community or caste lines. They may not vote on community and caste lines. The High Court cannot judicially pronounce on a democratic choice. That is for the voters to decide," Justice Bagchi said.The bench clarified that it could not rewrite the Constitution or the statute by introducing a rotation requirement that finds no mention in Articles 330 and 332 or the Delimitation Act.The Allahabad high court had held that Articles 330 and 332 merely prescribe the number of reserved seats in proportion to the population and leave the methodology for identifying reserved constituencies to Parliament under Article 327.It had found Section 9(1)(c) neither ultra vires nor violative of fundamental rights, ruling that courts cannot issue a mandamus directing the legislature to introduce a rotation provision.While acknowledging that rotation could better advance social and political justice by allowing SC/ST candidates to contest even from constituencies with smaller reserved-category populations, the high court had emphasised that the policy decision rests exclusively with Parliament.
Article Summary: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant quipped at a petitioner to organise public protests and demonstrations. He rejected his plea seeking mandatory rotation of seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Parliament and state assemblies. The Supreme Court said the petitioner was free to approach public representatives and persuade them to adopt the principle of rotation.

NEW DELHI: The Congress on Wednesday described the Centre's decision to extend Agniveers' service tenure by two years as a "U-turn", claiming it was driven by the upcoming assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Uttarakhand, where many young people aspire to join the armed forces."Elections are approaching in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, and Uttarakhand. A large number of youth from these states want to join the armed forces. So, they (government) took a U-turn out of fear," Congress MP Pawan Khera told ANI.Of the three states, the BJP, which leads the government at the Centre, will seek a third consecutive term in Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand.Reacting to the announcement by Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General NS Raja Subramani, Khera said the Congress had opposed the Agnipath scheme from the beginning as it would "adversely affect" the armed forces and the future of young recruits."We had opposed the Agniveer scheme right from the beginning. (LoP) Rahul Gandhi ji opposed it too. This scheme is harming not just our armed forces but also the youth of the country — you would leave them unemployed on the streets after another two years," he added.Questioning the Centre's revised arrangement, under which 25% of Agniveers would be absorbed into the regular forces based on merit while the remaining 75% would receive a two-year extension, the Congress MP asked what would happen to those who were not selected after the extended tenure."They say they'll absorb 25% into the army and give the rest a two-year extension. You'll absorb 25%. What will happen to the other 75%? After two years, will they be out on the streets again, or will you take another U-turn?" he asked.Earlier on Wednesday, CDS General Subramani announced that Agniveers who were previously required to leave after completing their four-year tenure would be offered an additional two-year engagement period.Those willing to join the armed forces would subsequently be enrolled based on objective selection criteria.The Agnipath scheme was introduced by the Union Cabinet in June 2022 for recruitment into the armed forces for a four-year tenure. Under the original arrangement, one-fourth of Agniveers were eligible for enrolment in the regular forces based on merit, while the remaining three-fourths would return to civilian life after completing their service.The revision announcement comes amid criticism of the scheme over the short duration of service and the employment prospects of recruits after leaving the armed forces.
Article Summary: The Congress described the Centre's decision to extend Agniveers' service tenure by two years as a "U-turn" Claimed it was driven by the upcoming assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Uttarakhand, where many young people aspire to join the armed forces.

Article Title: Centre proposes immediate suspension of licences for substandard drugs
Article Text:
The Health Ministry has introduced new regulations aimed at suspending manufacturing licenses for medicines that do not meet quality criteria. (Pic Credit: Magnific.com)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A medicine that fails critical quality tests could soon trigger immediate suspension of the manufacturer’s licence, under proposed rules aimed at preventing substandard drugs from reaching patients. Health ministry has proposed changes to the drugs rules, 1945, to allow regulators to act without waiting for the existing show-cause notice process.Currently, authorities follow a procedure that includes issuing a show-cause notice before suspending or cancelling a manufacturing licence. This can create a gap during which medicines declared ‘Not of standard quality (NSQ)’ may continue to circulate.Under the proposed amendments, central or state drug licensing authority can immediately suspend manufacturing licence for a drug if a govt analyst’s report finds it deficient in any of five critical parameters: assay, dissolution, related substances, impurities or sterility.These tests determine whether a medicine contains the required amount of active ingredient, releases it properly in the body and is free from harmful impurities or microbial contamination.The suspension will continue until the manufacturer identifies the reason for the quality failure and takes corrective and preventive action. The licence can be restored only after the regulatory authority verifies that the required measures have been implemented.The ministry has also proposed a system to ensure that reports of substandard drugs reach the drugs controller general of India (DCGI), the state or UT drug licensing authority concerned, and the manufacturer and marketer. This is intended to speed up regulatory action and fix accountability across the supply chain.The draft amendments have been opened for public consultation.
Article Summary: The Health Ministry has introduced new regulations aimed at suspending manufacturing licenses for medicines that do not meet quality criteria. Currently, authorities follow a procedure that includes issuing a show-cause notice before suspending or cancelling a manufacturing licence. This can create a gap during which medicines declared ‘Not of standard quality’ may continue to circulate.

Article Title: Changing NEET-PG to rank-based system won’t fix structural problems, doctors say
Article Text:
Altering the merit-list approach for NEET-PG and NEET-SS without resolving core structural issues proves to be insufficient. (Pic Credit: Magnific.com)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Changing NEET-PG and NEET-SS from a percentile-based to a rank-based system will not address the structural problems in medical education, doctors’ body said, flagging exorbitant fees, compulsory bonds, inadequate stipends and vacancies in less preferred specialities as the issues requiring urgent attention.“These were the key concerns raised by stakeholders at the October 9 DGHS meeting. Changing the merit-list methodology without addressing these issues is merely changing the approach, not reforming medical education,” United Doctors Front (UDF) chairperson Dr Lakshya Mittal who was part of the meeting said.The govt’s response to earlier stakeholder recommendations on these issues, reproduced in an expert committee report submitted to supreme court on Tuesday, points largely to state jurisdiction and existing regulations. On fee regulation, the govt cited NMC guidelines issued in February 2022 for determining charges for 50% of seats in private medical colleges and deemed universities, but said the guidelines were under litigation. Fee structures, it said, were governed by state regulatory authorities.On bonds, the govt said the policy fell under state jurisdiction. It also said stipends in National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences institutions were at par with those for MD/MS/DM/MCh seats in state institutions.Public-sector recruitment and job placements, it added, were also under state jurisdiction. These responses relate to earlier stakeholder recommendations and are not a direct reply to the October 9 meeting.At the meeting, Mittal had called for uniform fee regulation, bond-free admissions in pre-clinical and para-clinical branches, where seats often remain vacant, and equitable stipends. He also sought better faculty recruitment, career progression and research opportunities to address vacancies without resorting to zero or negative qualifying cut-offs.Other particpants in the meeting, Dr Raj Shekhar and Dr Ankit also flagged high fees, particularly in deemed universities, and sought fee regulatory committees to ensure reasonable charges. Participants called for uniform stipends across clinical and non-clinical branches and incentives for rural postings.Dr Nikhil questioned the basis for reducing qualifying percentiles in PG and super-speciality courses, including who took the decision and whether reductions should be restricted to the final counselling round. He also proposed independent audits of medical education costs.Participants cautioned against diluting qualifying standards merely to fill vacant seats. Dr G Raghavelu said measures to prevent seat wastage must protect professional standards. Biometric and KYC checks to prevent seat blocking were also suggested.The draft minutes record that qualifying marks could be reduced without compromising education quality, fees regulated uniformly through committees and stipends made more attractive. Separately, Supreme Court committee report records the NMC’s in-principle approval for a rank-based system for NEET-PG and NEET-SS, without declaring percentile marks. The proposal is yet to be formalised through regulations.
Article Summary: Doctors' body flags exorbitant fees, compulsory bonds, inadequate stipends and vacancies in less preferred specialities as the issues requiring urgent attention. Changing the merit-list methodology without addressing these issues is merely changing the approach, not reforming medical education, UDF chairperson Dr Lakshya Mittal said.

NEW DELHI: Imported medicines and medical devices could soon have more entry points into India, with the Centre proposing to add 10 locations to the country's authorised import network, including Noida International Airport and several inland container depots across key industrial hubs.The proposed expansion is expected to make it easier for companies to bring healthcare products into the country and clear consignments closer to their warehouses, manufacturing units and distribution centres, potentially reducing transportation costs and delays.Under a draft amendment to Drugs Rules, 1945, the health ministry has proposed adding ICDs at Sonipat, Piyala and Harsaru in Haryana; Dadri in Uttar Pradesh; Gandhidham/Mundra in Gujarat; Sanath Nagar and Thimmapur in Hyderabad; and Whitefield in Bengaluru. The Bommasandra Special Economic Zone in Karnataka has also been proposed as an entry point.Noida International Airport has been proposed specifically for the import of drugs by air.The proposed locations will supplement the existing authorised network, which includes ICDs at Dhannad and Tihi in Indore, along with notified airports and other entry points.At present, Rule specifies the ports, airports, railway stations, road crossings and other locations through which drugs can be imported into India. The proposed changes seek to widen this network to facilitate the movement and clearance of drugs, medical devices and cosmetics.The ministry has invited objections and suggestions on the draft amendment before finalising the changes. Responses can be sent to the Under Secretary (Drugs Regulation), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Article Summary: The proposed expansion is expected to make it easier for companies to bring healthcare products into the country. The proposed locations will supplement the existing authorised network, which includes ICDs at Dhannad and Tihi in Indore. Article Title: NDC draws line between general and specialist dental practice
Article Text:
The commission has asked state dental councils and tribunals to issue advisories or public notices clarifying the permitted scope of practice and preventing violations

NEW DELHI: A dentist's degree does not automatically qualify them to perform every dental procedure. The National Dental Commission (NDC) has clarified that practitioners must restrict their clinical work to procedures covered by their qualifications and specialised training, bringing the scope of general and specialist dental practice into focus.In an advisory, the commission's Ethics and Dental Registration Board said it had received queries from registered dentists seeking clarity on the permissible scope of practice. It said the BDS and Master of Dental Surgery (MDS) curricula define the competencies and procedures that each category of dentist is trained to perform.The BDS curriculum covers routine procedures such as fillings, simple root canals, uncomplicated extractions, dentures and basic orthodontic treatment. Graduates are also expected to identify complex cases and refer them to specialists. MDS provides advanced training in fields such as oral surgery, orthodontics, periodontology, prosthodontics and endodontics.For instance, BDS graduates are trained in simple orthodontic procedures and routine extractions, while complex corrective jaw surgeries and advanced oral surgeries require specialist expertise.Welcoming the clarification, (Hony.) Brig Anil Kohli, former president of the Dental Council of India and an endodontist, said the NDC should issue a procedure-wise list defining the scope of general and specialist practice.“Routine procedures such as fillings, scaling, simple extractions and basic root canals can be performed by competent BDS graduates, but complex implants, impacted wisdom tooth surgeries, corrective jaw procedures and advanced periodontal treatments must be reserved for trained MDS specialists.The dividing line should be clinical competence, not just the degree, with patient safety taking precedence,” he said.Kohli also called for mandatory continuing dental education for licence renewal, backed by clinical audits and action against violations. General dentists with recognised additional training should be allowed to expand their scope of practice, he said.“Dentists must be transparent about their qualifications, expertise and limitations, explain treatment risks and refer patients when necessary. Ensuring appropriate treatment is their responsibility, not the patient’s. Patient interests must always come first,” he saidThe commission has asked state dental councils and tribunals to issue advisories or public notices clarifying the permitted scope of practice and preventing violations.
Article Summary: The National Dental Commission has clarified that practitioners must restrict their clinical work to procedures covered by their qualifications and specialised training. The commission has asked state dental councils and tribunals to issue advisories or public notices clarifying the permitted scope of practice and preventing violations.

Article Title: A drug, custom-made in The Hague, for 7 kids in India
Article Text:
The drug, tiratricol, is goi­ng to be compounded by Tr­ansvaal Pharmacy for 1.8 euro per capsule (Representative image)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Dutch and Indian physicians and civil society organisations have come together to ensure access to a rare disease drug for seven children in India, by compounding the drug in the Hague and sending it to India. Compounding is the process by which a medicine is custom-made in small quantities.The drug, tiratricol, is going to be compounded by Transvaal Pharmacy for 1.8 euro per capsule, which is 99 times cheaper than the commercial drug sold by the Swedish company Egetis in Germany for 180 euro (over Rs 19,000) per tablet.Currently, the family of one of the children is importing the medicine from Germany. It costs them Rs 3 lakh per month. Since it is prescribed for life, buying it is proving to be unsustainable.The seven children suffer from a rare disease, Allan Herndon-Dudley Syndrome (AHDS), also known as MCT8 deficiency. Due to a genetic defect, their thyroid hormones are unable to reach their brain cells effectively, leading to severe developmental issues. Research by the Erasmus University Medical Centre (Erasmus MC) has confirmed that tiratricol, a medication known since 1953, could reduce the physical manifestations of the disease.Tiratricol has been in the market in France since 1974 to treat patients with thyroid conditions.In 2014, doctors at Erasmus MC, through research which involved 14 million euro of public funding, discovered that tiratricol could also be used to treat AHDS. Erasmus MC sold the intellectual property rights to Egetis without a “fair price clause”. In 2025, Egetis received European marketing authorisation for tiratricol, granting it 10 years of market exclusivity under the European orphan drug legislation. By 2026, the price per tablet of tiratricol had gone up from 0.35 euro, at which it was being sold in France in 2017, to almost 180 euro per tablet in Germany.The Netherland-based Pharmaceutical Accountability Foundation (PAF) which works to ensure access to medicines and medical technologies in a sustainable manner, is coordinating the effort to make the drug available to children in India. Wilbert Bannenberg of PAF termed Egetis’ pricing of tiratricol an “unethical business model”.A news report on the funding effort, which caught the attention of PAF, kicked off the Dutch-India collaboration.Since compounding by a pharmacy is only an emergency fix, for a long-term solution PAF is working with access to medicine activists and paediatricians in India for affordable production and registration of tiratricol in India, which could help start generic production in a few years.
Article Summary: The drug, tiratricol, is going to be compounded by Transvaal Pharmacy for 1.8 euro per capsule. It is 99 times cheaper than the commercial drug sold by the Swedish company Egetis in Germany for 180 euro per tablet. The seven children suffer from a rare disease, Allan Herndon-Dudley Syndrome.

Article Title: TFR down, need relook at popn control laws like 2-child norm for polls: SC

NEW DELHI: Observing that laws aimed at controlling population growth in the country had lost their significance because of a fall in the total fertility rate (TFR) from 3 to 1.9, below the replacement level of 2.1, Supreme Court Wednesday said the foundation of such laws had "crumbled", they had become "counter-productive" and their validity, which was upheld by it two decades ago, needed to be re-examined in the present situation.The court then decided to review its 2003 verdict for disqualifying individuals with more than two children from contesting elections to panchayati raj institutions.A bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said the earlier perception that population had a negative impact on development did not hold anymore, and not keeping the law abreast of changing times would have consequences far beyond the specific precedent or the law in question."Even though India's population is not yet declining, the TFR falling below the replacement rate will soon result in a demographic transition towards an older population with a declining share of the working-age population. Laws aimed at limiting population growth have now lost significance. If we fail to take note of such demographic changes, India will face serious consequences...," it said. Disqualification provisions on the basis of more than two children for local body polls have been in effect in various states. The court passed the order while examining the validity of a Maharashtra law which was challenged by a woman sarpanch. Article Title: UN report finds huge gap in adaptation finance ahead of COP31
Article Text:
The report was published ahead of the 31st session of the UN climate change conference (COP31) (Photo: PTI).

NEW DELHI: Even if the developed countries triple their money available to support developing nations to adapt to climate change by 2035, it would still cover less than a third of what is actually needed to protect people from disastrous consequences of global warming , the UN Environment Programme flagged in its annual Adaptation Gap Report on Wednesday.It estimates that the developing countries will need around $305 billion annually by 2035, or approximately $420 billion once future inflation is taken into account, to adapt themselves. But the collective pledge of the rich nations to triple international public finance flows could reach only $85-120 billion a year by 2035. So, this would only cover 20-29% of what the developing countries need to deal with intensifying climate impacts.If one looks at the actual contribution of rich nations in 2024, they provided only $28.2-31.7 billion in 2024, a $1 billion increase over the previous year. It practically means for every dollar developing countries need to adapt, they receive just 10 cents.“The world is not ready to adapt to current climatic conditions, never mind what overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius will bring,” said Inger Andersen, executive director of UNEP, referring to the inevitability of global warming exceeding the 1.5 degree C threshold (above 1850-1900 levels).Such warming has the potential to increase the number of extreme weather events, leading to worsening impacts of climate change.The report ahead of the 31st session of the UN climate change conference (COP31), scheduled to take place in Antalya, Turkiye, from Nov 9 to 20, may help negotiators from participating countries to put additional focus on adaptation finance.The report finds that adaptation finance continues to fall far short of needs, implementation remains constrained by institutional barriers, and loss and damage are mounting as climate impacts intensify. “Action on all these fronts is essential to build resilience in a rapidly changing climate,” it said.
Article Summary: The UN Environment Programme flagged in its annual Adaptation Gap Report on Wednesday. It estimates that the developing countries will need around $305 billion annually by 2035. The report was published ahead of the 31st session of the UN climate change conference (COP31)

Article Title: 'India will face serious consequences': SC on 'crumbling' fear of overpopulation
Article Text:
The Supreme Court held that a previous ruling from 1974 regarding additional sales tax remains applicable today.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday remarked that laws penalising people for having more than two children have "lost relevance", saying that the "fear of overpopulation" has "crumbled" due to "demographic changes over the past few decades. "A bench of Justices PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe made the observation while hearing a plea filed by Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, whose election as sarpanch of Maharashtra's Kakoda gram panchayat was set aside on the ground that she was disqualified from contesting the polls for having more than two children, in violation of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959.The bench referred the matter to a larger bench for reconsideration of the 2003 judgment in Javed versus State of Haryana. In that ruling, the Supreme Court had upheld the disqualification of people with more than two living children from contesting or holding panchayat positions under the Haryana Panchayati Raj Act, 1994."We are of the strong opinion that laws that penalise having more than two children have lost their relevance. The foundation of such laws, i.e. the fear of overpopulation, has crumbled due to demographic changes in the past few decades," PTI quoted the bench as saying.The judges noted that India's total fertility rate (TFR) had fallen from 3.0 in 2003 to 1.9, below the replacement rate of 2.1. It warned that this could lead to an ageing population and a decline in the share of the working-age population.The top court cautioned that ignoring these demographic changes could have "serious consequences" for the country.The bench further stated that the two-child policy laws "exclude" an entire section of citizens from political representation and force them to choose between having children and participating in democracy, infringing on their right to reproductive autonomy under Article 21."It would be dangerously complacent to ignore the consequences of India's changing population growth rate merely because it already has a large population -- the stakes are too high," it added.Warning of a potentially irreversible decline in fertility, the bench cautioned that India could soon face an ageing population with a disproportionately large share of people beyond working age.Referring to China's shift from its one-child policy to allowing three children, the bench highlighted the risks of treating declining fertility as a policy achievement."The Chinese experience therefore demonstrates the danger inherent in treating fertility reduction as a policy achievement capable of being calibrated at will," it said.Recalling its 2003 judgment in the Javed case, the court remarked: "We cannot ride into the future on a horse that is dead. It is not the strongest of the species that survives nor the most intelligent, but the most responsive to change."
Article Summary: Justices PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe made the observation while hearing a plea filed by Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, whose election as sarpanch of Maharashtra's Kakoda gram panchayat was set aside. The bench referred the matter to a larger bench for reconsideration of the 2003 judgment in Javed versus State of Haryana.

Article Title: Rank-based merit list to replace percentile for NEET PG: Panel to SC

NEW DELHI: Medical postgraduate admissions could see a major change, with the National Medical Commission (NMC) giving in-principle approval to replace the existing percentile-based system with a rank-based system for NEET-PG and NEET-Super Speciality (SS) counselling.A 12-member expert committee constituted to review the NEET-PG admission and counselling process told Supreme Court in its report on Tuesday that the commission is working on a new regulation under which only ranks would be declared and percentile marks would no longer be specified.The proposal received in-principle approval at the NMC's meeting on Sept 23, according to a letter dated Oct 1, 2026, from the NMC secretary to the director general of health services (DGHS). The commission is yet to finalise the regulation.SC is examining various petitions challenging Centre's decision to drastically reduce the qualifying cut-off percentiles for NEET-PG 2025. Under revised criteria, the qualifying score for general category was reduced from 276 to 103, while that for SC/ST/OBC categories was brought down from 235 to minus 40.The report was filed after detailed deliberations and consideration of suggestions made by senior advocate Maninder Singh, who is assisting the Supreme Court as amicus curiae."NMC is in process of issuing new regulations, which are yet to be finalised wherein only rank-based system for NEET PG & SS counselling will be adopted; no percentile marks will be declared in results; only ranks will be given to candidates. A letter dated Oct 1 has been written by secretary, NMC to DGHS informing proposal for changing existing percentile-based system to a rank-based merit system for NEET-PG and NEET-SS which is under consideration by the Commission.The panel has accorded in-principle approval for proposed change with a view to address the issues arising from the existing system," the report said.On reduction of minimum qualification, the report said, "sanctity of NEET examinations should be maintained and minimum qualifying standards in postgraduate medical education is not diluted to the extent of permitting candidates with grossly inadequate or negative performance to become eligible for admission; the significance of competitive examinations should not be reduced to an administrative formality. Article Summary: National Medical Commission (NMC) gives in-principle approval to replace existing percentile-based system. NMC is in process of issuing new regulations, which are yet to be finalised. No percentile marks will be declared in results; only ranks will be given to candidates.

Article Title: Watch: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay launches one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns
Article Text:
Vijay presented 22-carat, one-gram gold rings to 25 newborns. (PTI)

Who is eligible for the gold ring?

Scheme draws on Tamil tradition

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. He also held some of the newborns and presented the rings to beneficiaries during the launch programme.Under the scheme, eligible babies born in government hospitals and government primary health centres will receive a 22-carat, one-gram gold ring.The initiative, named the Maternal Uncle Gold Ring Scheme (Thaaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam), has an annual allocation of Rs 755.83 crore.It is aimed at celebrating motherhood, promoting maternal and child health and encouraging institutional deliveries by increasing public confidence in government healthcare facilities.The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions.Mothers must be registered under the Pregnancy and Infant Cohort Monitoring and Evaluation (PICME) system and have a Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) ID. They will also have to provide an e-KYC-verified Aadhaar card along with one of the prescribed identity or residence documents.These include ration cards, voter identity cards, Labour Welfare Board identity cards, Department of Posts address cards and nativity certificates.The state government has already procured 1.28 lakh one-gram gold rings for the initial rollout. Each ring will have a unique serial number and will be packed in tamper-proof packaging.From Monday, babies born in government hospitals will receive the rings at the time of discharge, according to the state government.To clear the backlog of eligible babies born between June 22 and Monday, the government will distribute the rings through 107 hubs across Tamil Nadu.Distribution will begin at the rate of 100 babies per day at each hub. At designated centres, 25 beneficiaries will be accommodated in the morning and another 25 in the afternoon to avoid overcrowding, PTI reported.Village Health Nurses will distribute invitations informing beneficiaries of their allotted date and time. Beneficiaries have been asked to visit the designated centres only at the time mentioned in their invitations.The district administration has also made transportation arrangements for beneficiaries from their respective areas. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election as a symbolic gift to newborns, drawing on the Tamil tradition of ‘Thaimaaman Seer’. The scheme has retrospective effect from June 22, Vijay’s birthday.A government order issued on June 23 described the initiative as a token celebrating the birth of a child, motherhood and the cultural tradition of ‘Thaimaaman’.According to ANI, Tamil Nadu minister Arun Raj explained the cultural significance of the initiative saying, "A maternal uncle is someone who is among the first to rush in when a child is born, sharing in his sister’s happiness as his own. He assures her that he will always stand by her and her child, offering love, support and a sense of security.""Today, the Tamil Nadu Government, under the leadership of our brother, Mr. Vijay, is embracing this sacred bond of the maternal uncle and, as a gesture of that affection, is set to provide a one-gram gold ring to every child born in government hospitals. When the scheme was announced and the question arose as to where it should be launched, the place chosen by our Chief Minister was Madurai. This is the sacred soil of Madurai, blessed with the compassion and grace of Mother Meenakshi," he added.Tamil Nadu records around 7.8 lakh deliveries annually, with institutional deliveries accounting for 99.9% of births, according to NFHS-6. Government health facilities account for nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries, or around 53% of the total.According to the state government, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a delivery at a government hospital is Rs 1,364, compared with Rs 63,473 at a private hospital.The government said the scheme is intended to encourage safe institutional deliveries, strengthen maternal and child welfare and increase public trust in government healthcare services.The Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation will procure the gold rings based on annual requirements, while a project and programme management unit will oversee implementation and monitoring.
Article Summary: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election.

Article Title: Delhi landfill garbage mountains shrinking, 100 acres reclaimed in 18 months: CM Rekha Gupta
Article Text:
Delhi CM Rekha Gupta poses for a group picture during an on-site inspection of waste disposal operations near Okhla, in New Delhi

Government targets legacy and fresh waste

New processing plants at three sites

NEW DELHI: Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the garbage mountains at the city's landfill sites were steadily shrinking as she reviewed waste disposal work at Okhla and laid the foundation stone for new waste processing facilities at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola.Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years, with a large portion of the cleared area also being turned green.She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed."Today, at Okhla, we have processed almost all the legacy waste that was there before January 2025," Gupta said.Gupta said the government was working on two fronts: clearing the existing garbage mountains while ensuring that fresh waste generated every day did not accumulate into new landfill sites.According to news agency ANI, she said around 3,000-4,000 metric tonnes of fresh waste reaches the sites daily and is being processed round the clock."The garbage currently piled up here is essentially fresh waste generated after January 2025, and that too is being processed round the clock. So, we are fighting on two fronts: one is eliminating waste, and the other is ensuring that the 3,000 to 4,000 metric tons of fresh waste arriving daily is processed immediately, so that new garbage mountains are not formed for future generations," Gupta said.She said the government was working to reduce the existing garbage mountains to zero."People are seeing that the garbage mountains are continuously shrinking and soon a time will come when they will become zero," Gupta said.Gupta also said she had taken what she described as her "last selfie" with the garbage mountain at Okhla."Today I have taken my last selfie with the garbage mountain; after this I have taken a pledge that this garbage mountain will end soon," she said.Taking a jibe at the Opposition, Gupta added, "I had said - garbage mountain, you will have to go; the opposition mocked. Today I will say the garbage mountain is going; now only its back remains."During the programme at the Okhla SLF site, Gupta laid the foundation stone for fresh waste processing plants at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola, as well as a biogas facility at Ghazipur. She also inaugurated the M&CW Centre at Kotla Mubarakpur through virtual mode from Okhla.The Okhla plant will be built at a cost of Rs 103 crore and will have a processing capacity of 1,400 metric tonnes per day.The Singhola facility will cost Rs 42 crore and have a capacity of 800 metric tonnes per day, while the Ghazipur plant will have a processing capacity of 700 metric tonnes per day.The facilities are intended to process fresh waste as well as construction and demolition waste. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure."Waste should not remain waste; Delhi should use it as wealth," she said, adding that new technologies were being introduced for waste segregation and processing.She said waste and cattle dung would be used to produce biogas and manure as part of efforts to build a technology-driven waste management system.Gupta said the government was taking up several measures to address pollution, including work on landfill waste, cleaning the Yamuna, dust mitigation, plantation, road infrastructure and waste management."Our government is tackling pollution from a 360-degree perspective to ensure it gradually decreases. We are working on every aspect, be it addressing the mountains of garbage, cleaning the Yamuna, improving road infrastructure, or managing waste, to ensure the people of Delhi enjoy better air quality. Our resolve and policies are absolutely clear, and we are working 24x7 in the public interest," she said.The chief minister also reviewed the progress of waste disposal work with officials and directed them to accelerate the work according to the stipulated timeline.She said the garbage mountains at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla had caused inconvenience to people travelling through these areas and said the government was continuing efforts to eliminate them.
Article Summary: Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years. She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure.

Article Title: India-US trade talks hit ‘plateau’: Sitharaman says further give-and-take ‘very, very difficult’
Article Text:
Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman

India stresses strategic autonomy in trade negotiations

India-EU pact opens market access

India and US have reached a “plateau” in negotiations over their bilateral trade agreement, with further concessions from either side likely to be "very very difficult", finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday. Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi, she said that while negotiations are still underway, any progress from here would depend on whether there was limited room for compromise on either side.“The agreement negotiations are still ongoing, although we'd like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult. But maybe if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it,” Sitharaman said.She said the agreement was still being “hard and very rigorously negotiated” and that India has a trade surplus with the US. “But what is the predominant feature of the trade relations between India and the US? The trade balance is very much in our favor.”Sitharaman said that the US would naturally want to reduce this trade imbalance and address what it sees as losses built up over the years.She also said that the way countries negotiate trade deals was changing, with governments now looking beyond traditional negotiations to address trade imbalances.“Negotiation used to be the only platform through which countries could highlight the discrepancies, highlight the lop-sidedness and say, would we want to correct this?” she said.“Tariff was an instrument of negotiation, and tariff had a certain framework within which you will apply it. Today framework is there, tariffs are going,” she said, while stressing that countries still need to negotiate and find “some give and take”.Sitharaman was also asked about maintaining strategic autonomy while negotiating bilateral trade agreements with European countries, including in the context of India procuring Russian oil."There is no Lindsay Graham Bill in Europe...," she said.On the broader question of how bilateral trade agreements can protect a country's interests in an era of multilateralism, Sitharaman said countries were increasingly choosing bilateral partnerships where they saw greater benefit.“Countries choose where multilateralism would benefit them, and there are some unique bilaterals which countries choose to have. The balance is somewhat tilted in favour of the bilateral rather than the multilateral,” she said.She said countries were now increasingly looking for new trade partners and strengthening those relationships through agreements.“Countries are now rapidly catching up with — I would put the EU-India also in a bilateral mode -because it's one in the name of union, but of course within them they have. So, bilaterals today are catching up far more than even initiating or beginning a multilateral. It's not deliberate, but in a way, if you don't do it, you're not moving forward. Countries will have to choose new partners for their trade and strengthen the tie through an agreement. And therefore, newer partnerships are being searched for, and they are tied up bilaterally.”FM Sitharaman cited the India-EU trade agreement as a major example of India's approach to negotiating trade pacts while protecting domestic interests.She said India had opened 92.5 per cent of its tariff lines and around 97 per cent of tariff value under the agreement. The EU, meanwhile, had opened 99 per cent in value terms and possibly 97 per cent of tariff lines.According to Sitharaman, greater access to the European market could support employment in labour-intensive sectors, including footwear, textiles, toys and processed products. Many of these sectors are linked to micro and small enterprises.“Those are all in the micro and small medium industry segment, which are labor-intensive,” Sitharaman said, adding that greater access to the European market could generate “more exports, more jobs”.Sitharaman said bilateral trade agreements were becoming increasingly important as multilateral institutions have weakened.“Multilateralism is not going to go away. But multilateralism has weakened,” she said.She also stressed that multilateralism should continue even as countries increasingly pursue bilateral agreements.“Multilateralism is not going to go away and multilateralism shouldn't go away,” Sitharaman said.The Munich Leaders Meeting, being held in the National Capital, provides a platform for about 100 senior decision-makers and experts to discuss opportunities for stronger cooperation among emerging and middle powers amid profound geopolitical change. Discussions include geoeconomic developments, trade and connectivity, maritime security, defence cooperation and other key international challenges.
Article Summary: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman says India and US have reached a 'plateau' in negotiations over their bilateral trade agreement. She said any progress from here would depend on whether there was limited room for compromise on either side. She also said the way countries negotiate trade deals was changing, with governments now looking beyond traditional negotiations to address trade imbalances.
