Jio IPO

Jio IPO: Jio Platforms' $3.2 billion initial public offering (IPO) was fully subscribed within less than two hours of bidding opening on Wednesday, as investors rushed to participate in India's biggest-ever share sale. The offering is also the first IPO from billionaire Mukesh Ambani 's Reliance group in two decades.According to a PTI report, the Jio IPO was fully subscribed within 100 minutes of its opening on October 21.The rapid subscription was notable because large IPOs in India often see a slow start, with institutional investors typically placing their bids closer to the closing deadline. By comparison, the National Stock Exchange of India's share sale recently attracted subscriptions for just 42% of the shares on offer on its first day. Hyundai Motor India's IPO had received bids for only 18% of its offering on the opening day.Also Read | Jio IPO, India’s largest public issue, opens for subscription: Price band, GMP to brokerage views - top 10 things to know The IPO is open to retail investors, employees and eligible Reliance shareholders. The issue will close on Friday, with shares priced in a band of Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119 apiece.Exchange data showed that institutional investors had bid for 3.25 times the shares reserved for them by Wednesday. Retail participation was lower at that stage, with individual investors applying for 0.22 times their reserved quota.Retail investors have been allocated around one-third of the total offering.The IPO values Jio Platforms at as much as $108.3 billion. Once trading begins on October 28, the company could rank among India's largest listed companies by market capitalisation.Earlier this week, Jio Platforms allotted shares worth $853 million to domestic and international investors, including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and BlackRock. The anchor investor portion attracted bids exceeding $25 billion, according to a Reuters report.Backed by global investors such as Meta, Google's parent company Alphabet and other institutional investors, Jio Platforms houses India's largest telecom operator. With more than 500 million subscribers, the business is the world's second-largest telecom operator within a single country, behind China Mobile.This is Reliance's first IPO since 2006. Jio Platforms' telecom business, led by Ambani's son Akash, began operations in 2016. Its strategy was built around the expectation that Indians would use the internet much more extensively if access became almost free. By offering inexpensive data and free voice calls, Jio quickly gained market share from competitors such as Bharti Airtel and Vodafone Idea.
Article Summary: Jio IPO was fully subscribed within 100 minutes of its opening on October 21. The rapid subscription was notable because large IPOs in India often see a slow start. The IPO is open to retail investors, employees and eligible Reliance shareholders. The issue will close on Friday, with shares priced in a band of Rs 1,065 to Rs1,119 apiece.

Article Title: LPG consumption down, diesel & petrol sales up in September
Article Text:
LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier

NEW DELHI: LPG demand fell by over 9% year-on-year in Sept, while petrol and diesel sales registered growth of 7% and 5%, respectively, provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) showed.LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier.Month-on-month consumption, however, registered a growth of 8%, up from 2.4 MT.Petrol sales increased from 3.4 MT in Sept last year to 3.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose from 6.8 MT to 7.1 MT. Petrol and diesel consumption had registered year-on-year growth of 7.9% and 6.5%, respectively, in July.While petrol is largely used as an automobile fuel and its consumption is commensurate with the increasing number of vehicles, diesel is consumed by transport vehicles for passenger and freight movement, besides being used in the agricultural sector.Erratic monsoon conditions due to El Nino boosted demand for diesel for irrigation.Cumulative petrol consumption during Apr-Sept in the current financial year increased 7% to 22.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose 4.8% to 47.9 MT. In contrast, LPG consumption declined 14.9% to 13.8 MT from 16.2 MT during the corresponding period of 2025-26.
Article Summary: LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier. Petrol sales increased from 3.4 MT in Sept last year to 3.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose from 6.8 MT to 7.1 MT.

Article Title: In 2009, Michael Jackson left a trust for his three children; 17 years later, daughter Paris is asking a court to move $600 million into it, while estate executors say unresolved tax litigation preven
Article Text:
Paris Jackson seeks $600 million from her father’s estate as a trust funding dispute raises questions about her brothers’ inheritance.

What Paris says was promised

Paris Jackson and Michael Jackson (Image Source: Left – Instagram/@parisjackson)

Why Paris wants $600 million

Paris Jackson files new documents in court and demands USD 600 million from her father’s estate; she alleges money has been withheld from being given to her and her siblings. She alleges that the executor of her father's estate has full control over how she and her siblings get the money and how much is transferred despite the clear declaration in Michael Jackson's will. (Instagram)

The estate’s response

Michael Jackson regularly hosted children and families at Neverland, including groups supported by charitable organisations such as the Make-A-Wish Foundation. (Photo: Instagram)

A wider family and estate conflict

What happens next

Michael Jackson

Seventeen years after Michael Jackson’s death, his daughter Paris Jackson has returned to court with a blunt request: move $600 million from the late singer’s estate into the family trust created for his three children. In a petition filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court, Paris argues that the Michael Jackson Family Trust remains unfunded despite the estate generating billions of dollars through music deals, property sales and other business ventures, reported LA Times. The estate’s executors have pushed back, saying they cannot fully fund the trusts until several legal matters are resolved, including a long-running dispute with the Internal Revenue Service. According to PEOPLE, the IRS initially sought about $700 million in taxes and penalties, although the estate says a ruling significantly reduced that amount. The matter has not been settled, and the estate argues it could still change.At the centre of the dispute is a familiar question in celebrity estates: when a fortune grows far beyond what anyone expected, how quickly should the beneficiaries receive what was promised to them? Paris says the answer is now.The estate says the answer must wait until the tax exposure and other legal risks are clearer. Read more details about this incident here, as per the reports.Michael Jackson died in June 2009 at age 50, leaving behind three children: Prince, Paris and Bigi. Paris, now 28, says the trust was designed to give each child income from their share when they turned 21, followed by portions of the principal at 30 and additional distributions at 35 and 40.Her filing says that arrangement has not operated as intended. Prince is 29 and approaching 30, Paris turns 29 in April, and Bigi turns 25 in February. According to Paris, none of them has begun receiving the trust distributions contemplated by the estate plan, leaving them reliant on discretionary payments controlled by the estate’s remaining executor, John Branca. “More than seventeen years after his passing, Michael Jackson’s family trust remains unfunded,” the petition states, as quoted by PEOPLE. Paris also alleges that the executors said in 2011 that they would seek court approval to begin funding the trust, but that no such petition was ever filed.Paris’s legal team argues that the estate has more than enough liquidity to make a substantial partial distribution. The petition points to the 2018 sale of the estate’s interest in EMI Music Publishing for $287.5 million, the $22 million sale of Neverland Ranch in 2020, and a major 2023 deal with Sony involving Michael’s music and other intellectual-property assets.Those transactions reportedly generated more than $1 billion in cash before taxes and expenses. Paris’s filing also cites an estate accounting showing approximately $850 million in cash and cash-equivalent assets as of December 2024. After accounting for potential liabilities, her lawyers conclude that roughly $600 million is available for distribution.The petition asks the court to order a preliminary transfer of $600 million to the Michael Jackson Family Trust, or another amount the judge considers appropriate. Paris argues that the estate’s executors have kept the beneficiaries dependent on them by controlling when and how much money is distributed.The estate denies that it has withheld money or reduced payments to the children. In a statement to PEOPLE, it called that allegation “a complete fabrication” and said more than $200 million had already been distributed for their benefit.It also pointed to the terms of Michael’s will, saying that none of his children receives a distribution until they are in their 30s. The estate said it looks forward to fully funding the children’s trusts once all issues are resolved, but insisted that outstanding legal matters must be addressed first.The IRS case is the largest unresolved issue. The estate says the tax dispute, which initially involved about $700 million in taxes and penalties, has been reduced by a court ruling but remains unsettled. Because the final liability could still change, the estate argues that moving hundreds of millions of dollars into the trust now would be premature.The request is not happening in isolation. Paris has previously challenged aspects of the estate’s administration, and her latest petition alleges that her objections were met with public criticism, litigation and a multimillion-dollar reduction in payments to her and her brothers.Earlier this year, a Los Angeles judge ruled that $625,000 in bonus payments made by the estate’s executors to outside law firms in 2018 had to be returned to the estate. The ruling came after Paris objected to the payments. Attorneys for the estate disagreed with the decision but said they would comply with it.Following Michael’s death, Branca and John McClain were appointed co-executors of his estate and oversaw its affairs for several years. McClain’s death in May 2026 left Branca as the sole executor. The estate has continued to earn substantial revenue from Michael’s work while dealing with several legal disputes.A judge is scheduled to hear Paris’s request on December 4. The hearing will not necessarily resolve the entire dispute, but it will determine whether the court believes a partial transfer to the family trust is justified before the estate’s outstanding legal matters are fully resolved.For the Jackson children, the case is about access to money their father intended to provide. For the estate, it is about protecting assets against a tax bill that could still move substantially. Both sides agree that Michael wanted his children provided for. They disagree sharply on whether the estate has honoured that intention, and on whether $600 million can safely be released now.What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments section below.
Article Summary: Michael Jackson died in June 2009 at age 50, leaving behind three children: Prince, Paris and Bigi. Paris, now 28, says the trust was designed to give each child income from their share when they turned 21, followed by portions of the principal at 30 and additional distributions at 35 and 40. Her filing says that arrangement has not operated as intended. The estate says the answer must wait until the tax exposure and other legal risks are clearer.

Article Title: A Wyoming landowner had 640 acres with no legally usable road to reach them; after a neighbouring ranch resisted access, the state’s highest court approved a private road but upheld $61,200 in compens
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

The dispute over access to 640 acres

Why the property was considered landlocked

The $61,200 compensation award

Changes to the private road conditions

Final ruling and its implications

A 640-acre property is of little practical use if its owner cannot legally reach it by vehicle. That problem became the centre of a dispute between two Wyoming landowners after Wagonhound Land & Livestock Company sought access to an isolated parcel surrounded almost entirely by a neighbouring ranch. After negotiations failed, the company approached the court to establish a private road across the neighbouring property, but the ranch challenged the move and disputed the compensation.In its September 23, 2026, decision in Wagonhound Land & Livestock Company, LLC v. Little Medicine Creek Ranch, Inc., available on Justia, the Wyoming Supreme Court upheld the creation of the private road and the $61,200 compensation awarded to the neighbouring ranch. However, it overturned two restrictions imposed on the road, finding that they lacked sufficient supporting evidence.The dispute concerned Parcel 1, a roughly 640-acre tract in a remote and rugged part of northern Albany County, Wyoming. The property belonged to Wagonhound and was surrounded almost entirely by land owned by Little Medicine Creek Ranch, formerly known as Burnett Ranch.On April 21, 2023, Wagonhound sent the ranch a letter expressing interest in purchasing legally enforceable access to the isolated property.It proposed a 30-foot-wide right-of-way along existing ranch roads and indicated that it was willing to negotiate a fair price. However, the discussions failed to produce an agreement. Wagonhound subsequently filed a petition under Wyoming's private road statute, seeking permission to establish access across the neighbouring ranch.Little Medicine Creek Ranch opposed the request, arguing that Wagonhound already had an outlet through adjoining Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land and could use an alternative route to reach a public road.The ranch argued that an existing two-track route across BLM land provided Wagonhound with access. However, the route eventually crossed state trust land and required passage through approximately 1,700 feet of the neighbouring ranch's private property. The Wyoming Supreme Court found that the existence of a rough track across public land did not, by itself, establish legally enforceable access to a public road. There was no evidence that the general public had used the route, and access to it was effectively controlled by the surrounding private property.The ranch also proposed the Parsons Creek Route, suggesting Wagonhound could obtain permission to construct a bypass across public land. However, that road did not physically exist. BLM employees also questioned whether the proposed route was accessible, while witnesses described parts of it as little more than a trail. The court concluded that neither option provided legally enforceable vehicle access to a public road. It therefore agreed that Wagonhound had established the necessity for a private road.The district court appointed three independent viewers and appraisers to examine possible routes and assess the impact on the neighbouring property. They recommended Wagonhound's proposed route because it was shorter, more direct and more practical than the alternative suggested by the ranch. The alternative would require construction across a rocky ridge and could make winter access difficult.The viewers estimated that the private road would affect 680 acres of the neighbouring ranch. Using comparable property sales and an earlier appraisal report, they calculated a reduction in value of $90 per acre. This resulted in a total compensation award of $61,200, which the district court approved. Little Medicine Creek Ranch challenged the calculation, arguing that the assessment did not account for potential operational losses, including livestock health problems linked to dust, additional staffing expenses and reduced hunting opportunities.However, the Supreme Court upheld the award. It explained that Wyoming's private road statute requires a before-and-after appraisal to determine the reduction in the value of the affected property. It does not provide compensation for indirect future business losses. The court also noted that the ranch had not presented evidence disputing the viewers' calculation of the affected acreage or the $90-per-acre reduction.Although the court upheld the private road and compensation, it overturned two conditions imposed by the district court. The first required Wagonhound to pay for any damage to the road, regardless of whether its own vehicles, the neighbouring ranch or their guests had caused it. The Supreme Court found no evidence justifying this requirement. Wagonhound remained responsible for maintaining the road for its use, but could not automatically be held liable for damage caused by others.The second restriction prohibited vehicles with more than four axles, including semi-trailers, from using the road. The court found insufficient evidence that heavy vehicles would create unreasonable noise, lighting problems or other disturbances. However, it upheld the requirement that Wagonhound regularly apply water to suppress dust, citing evidence about its potential impact on livestock. The court also rejected the ranch's request to restrict the road exclusively to agricultural use, finding insufficient evidence to justify such a limitation.On September 23, 2026, the Wyoming Supreme Court affirmed the findings on necessity, good faith, route selection and compensation, while reversing parts of two road conditions. The decision allows Wagonhound to obtain legally enforceable vehicle access to its 640-acre property while requiring it to pay the neighbouring ranch $61,200. It also clarifies that a landowner cannot be denied access simply because a rough track crosses public land when no legally usable connection to a public road exists.The ruling was therefore partly in favour of both parties: Wagonhound secured the private road, while Little Medicine Creek Ranch retained its compensation and dust-control protections. For landowners dealing with isolated parcels, the decision highlights the importance of establishing a legally recognised route to public roads, rather than relying on informal tracks or uncertain access arrangements.
Article Summary: The dispute concerned Parcel 1, a roughly 640-acre tract in a remote and rugged part of northern Albany County, Wyoming. The property belonged to Wagonhound Land & Livestock Company and was surrounded almost entirely by land owned by Little Medicine Creek Ranch. After negotiations failed, the company approached the court to establish a private road across the neighbouring property, but the ranch challenged the move and disputed the compensation.

Article Title: Diwali bonanza on Dalal Street! Sensex settles 2,000 points higher, investors end Rs 8 lakh crore richer; top reasons behind stock market rally
Article Text:
Fireworks on Dalal Street

Here are the top reasons behind market rally:

1. Crude oil prices slide below $95

2. US midterm election results improve global sentiment

3. Foreign investors return to Dalal Street

4. Rupee touches two-week high

5. Broader markets and banking stocks join the rally

(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market and other asset classes given by experts are their own. These opinions do not represent the views of The Times of India)

Stock market today: Dalal Street brought an early Diwali bonanza for investors on Thursday, with Sensex soaring over 2,100 points and Nifty50 gaining over 2%. Both benchmarks delivered their biggest single day gains in seven months, with Rs 8.20 lakh crore added to investors' wealth. The momentum came amid easing crude oil prices, renewed foreign investor buying and improving global sentiment following the US midterm election results lifted market mood.The 30-share BSE Sensex surged 2,008.61 points, or 2.60%, to close at 79,310.01, while the NSE Nifty50 jumped 576 points, or 2.40%, to settle at 24,536.60.Dalal Street extended its winning streak to six consecutive sessions on Thursday, building on Wednesday's gains when the Sensex climbed nearly 384 points to close at 77,301, its highest level in more than two months. NSE Nifty also advanced 150 points to settle at 23,961. The five-session rally through Wednesday had already lifted Sensex by over 4,000 points, or 5%.Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, told ANI, "The sharp advance reflects improving global risk sentiment, supported by lower crude prices and renewed institutional buying.”Falling crude oil prices remained one of the biggest factors supporting domestic equities on Thursday.Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, slipped below $95 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell below $90.Brent crude futures declined 50 cents, or 0.53%, to $94.12 per barrel, while WTI crude fell 61 cents, or 0.69%, to $87.51.The latest decline followed a sharp sell-off on Wednesday, when both benchmarks lost more than 8% and settled at their lowest levels in over two months. Brent ended the session at $94.62 per barrel, shedding $8.98, or 8.7%, whileThe decline in oil prices offered relief to India, as the economy is dependent on oil imports, and supported sentiment in domestic equities.The outcome of the November 2026 US midterm elections also contributed to the positive mood across markets.The Democratic Party won control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, dealing a significant political setback to US President Donald Trump's administration.The election outcome raised expectations that Trump could face greater pressure to bring the US-Israeli war with Iran to an end. With Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress, the US President could also find it harder to pursue further military action.Hopes of an end to the conflict supported the decline in crude oil prices and improved global risk sentiment.Vinod Nair, head of research, Geojit Investments Limited, told ANI, "The US midterm outcome improved global sentiment, raising expectations of a more measured approach to trade and tariff policies and potentially supporting FII flows into emerging markets,"Renewed buying by foreign institutional investors (FIIs) provided fresh support to domestic markets, with overseas investors purchasing Indian shares worth Rs 72.84 billion ($769.65 million) on Wednesday, marking their fourth consecutive session of buying.Foreign investors also pumped around Rs 17,235 crore into Indian equities in the first three trading sessions of November, signalling a revival in overseas institutional flows.The return of foreign money comes amid concerns over sustained capital outflows and India's long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax structure, which has emerged as a key concern for investors. This comes as market experts have been asking government to consider scrapping LTCG tax across investor categories.Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Monday said that she would consider concerns raised by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) over the capital gains tax framework, amid demands for a reduction in LTCG tax on equities. "The situation is very different now. Circumstances have changed. Challenges have grown. More net FII outflows have happened. It's started resuming now. They've started coming back now. So I know that circumstances have changed and therefore voices of concern are louder. I quite appreciate that. I'll consider all this,” the FM said.Rupee also extended its gains against the US dollar, opening at a two-week high of 94.35 per dollar on Thursday, up 0.3% from its previous close.The currency rose 14 paise to 94.32 against the US dollar in early trade, after closing at 95.64 on Wednesday, marginally stronger than its previous close of 95.75.This marked the fifth consecutive session of gains for the currency.Meanwhile, the dollar index, which measures the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was trading at 101.18, down 0.53%.Thursday's rally was broad-based, with buying seen across market segments, sectors and heavyweight stocks. Fourteen of the 16 major sectors ended in positive territory, while the broader mid-cap and small-cap indices also gained over 1% each.The Nifty Midcap 100 advanced 1.46%, while the Nifty Smallcap 100 rose 1.49%. The Nifty 100 also climbed 1.78%, reflecting the wider market rally.Among sectoral indices, Nifty Private Bank led the gains, rising 2.55%, followed by Nifty Realty at 1.92%. Nifty IT advanced 1.72%, Nifty Auto gained 1.66%, Nifty Consumer Durables rose 1.52% and Nifty Media climbed 1.36%. Nifty FMCG also ended 1.08% higher.On the Sensex, Bajaj Finance jumped 5.33%. Maruti Suzuki followed with a 4.94% rise, while InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo) gained 4.88%. Asian Paints advanced 4.39%, M&M rose 3.89% and Infosys climbed 3.67%.Other notable gainers included Tech Mahindra (3.35%), HCL Technologies (3.13%), UltraTech Cement (2.88%), TCS (2.87%), ICICI Bank (2.81%) and Bajaj Finserv (2.63%).The latest gains extend the momentum seen over the previous week. Earlier on Wednesday, Sensex climbed 383.55 points, or 0.50%, to close at 77,301.40, its highest closing level in more than two months. NSE Nifty50 advanced 149.75 points, or 0.63%, to settle at 23,960.60. Among Sensex constituents, Bharat Electronics, Titan, InterGlobe Aviation, Bajaj Finance, ITC and Adani Ports were the biggest gainers, while TCS, HCL Tech, Infosys and Eternal featured among the laggards.However, Ponmudi cautioned that sustaining the gains beyond the initial trading hours would be key to determining whether the rally could develop into a broader market recovery. He also noted that the sharp correction in crude oil prices offered some much-needed relief to India as an oil-import-dependent economy.
Article Summary: Sensex and Nifty50 deliver their biggest single day gains in seven months. Crude oil prices, renewed foreign investor buying and improving global sentiment lifted market mood. Rupee touches two-week high against US dollar, opening at a two-year high.

Article Title: Elon Musk's nearly $500 million US midterm gamble backfires: Tesla, SpaceX stocks take a hit
Article Text:
Musk's political gamble falls flat, Tesla, SpaceX stocks take a hit

Why Musk's businesses could feel the political heat

Where Musk's $474 million election money went

Musk was not the only tech billionaire backing Trump

Elon Musk poured nearly half a billion dollars into the US midterm elections, but lost the gamble. As Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress and Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott in the Texas governor's race, shares of Musk-owned companies came under pressure.Shares of Musk-owned companies came under pressure, with SpaceX falling 3.8% in premarket trading and Tesla slipping 3.6%. Both stocks underperformed the broader market.The decline came even as US equities rallied following the midterm elections. The S&P 500 jumped 1.6%, gaining 119.7 points to close at 7,688.62. The Nasdaq Composite added 364.50 points, or 1.4%, to 25,736.51, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average surged 1,569.40 points, or 3%, to 53,356.12. The Dow rose more than 1,500 points during the session.US stocks have historically tended to gain following midterm elections, regardless of which party wins. However, Musk's businesses moved in the opposite direction as the election results dealt a blow to the Republicans and US President Donald Trump, a close ally whom the billionaire helped elect.The setback is particularly significant given Musk's business interests in Texas, which houses his electric vehicle maker Tesla, his rocket-to-AI company SpaceX and a planned chipmaking venture between the two.His election spending was aimed at helping Republican candidates retain their positions and keeping Texas red.An analysis by The New York Times suggests that Musk contributed $474 million to Republican candidates during the 2026 midterms, including almost $224 million in Texas alone, making him the biggest donor of the election by a considerable margin.The Democratic victory could have significant implications for Musk's companies, particularly SpaceX's plans to build data centres. Slower approvals for these facilities could become a major hurdle as the company looks to tap the $28.5 trillion addressable market it presented to investors ahead of its IPO.With Democrats now controlling both chambers of Congress, analysts and experts expect greater scrutiny of data-centre projects and possible pushes for construction moratoriums amid growing local opposition over electricity costs.Musk has already faced scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over restrictions on satellite communications used by Ukraine, mass federal job cuts at DOGE, and government contracts and subsidies flowing to his companies. The stronger Democratic presence in Congress could bring these issues back into focus.The latest market reaction also comes after a strong recovery in Tesla shares. The stock has rallied 34% since its late-July low, supported by investor optimism surrounding its artificial intelligence products and the potential combination with SpaceX.SpaceX, meanwhile, entered the ranks of the world's most valuable companies after going public earlier this year. The company generates billions of dollars through US government contracts, but its shares have largely remained flat since its June IPO, holding on to a massive $1.9 trillion market valuation.Musk's companies have previously shown sensitivity to election outcomes. Following Trump's re-election in 2024, Tesla shares surged more than 90% in little over a month. However, those gains later unwound as Musk's relationship with Trump soured and investors grew tired of his involvement in the Department of Government Efficiency.A significant portion of Musk's election spending flowed through political action committees supporting Republican candidates across the country.His America PAC, the super PAC he owns, received $216 million and was active in more than 40 House and Senate races. According to Newsweek, Musk contributed another $77 million to the group in the first half of October alone.The Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Senate Republicans, received $168 million. Of this amount, $158 million was passed on to Texas PAC, the biggest supporter of Republican Ken Paxton.Musk also contributed $30 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund to help protect the Republican majority in the House. His trust gave another $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, the main outside group supporting Paxton.His involvement in Republican fundraising is not new. In 2024, Musk spent nearly $300 million backing Trump and other Republican candidates.Musk's political contributions were the largest among four technology billionaires who backed Trump. Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, Michael Dell and Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff also supported the president through financial contributions, charitable commitments and White House projects.Ellison contributed around $45 million to a nonprofit supporting Trump's 2024 campaign, according to The Wall Street Journal. The donation remained undisclosed until June 2026. He later praised Trump at the White House event announcing the Stargate AI project, telling him, "We certainly couldn’t do this without you". Trump described Ellison as the "CEO of everything".Michael Dell and his wife Susan pledged $6.25 billion to fund "Trump Accounts". The money will go to the US Treasury and be deposited in $250 amounts into accounts for 25 million children aged 10 or younger. The programme targets children in zip codes where the median income is $150,000 or less. Trump later urged Americans to buy Dell computers, following which the company's stock rose more than 7%.Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff also backed Trump, marking a shift from his earlier political contributions, a major share of which went to Democrats. He committed $1 million towards Trump's White House ballroom, while Salesforce separately made two commitments of $1 million each. Benioff later faced criticism for supporting the deployment of National Guard troops in San Francisco, a proposal opposed by local city leaders. He subsequently withdrew his remarks and apologised for calling in the Guard.
Article Summary: Elon Musk poured nearly half a billion dollars into the US midterm elections. As Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress, shares of Musk-owned companies came under pressure. SpaceX fell 3.8% in premarket trading and Tesla slipped 3.6%. Both stocks underperformed the broader market.

Article Title: Bengaluru landlord withholds tenant's Rs 80,000 security deposit, claiming he failed to give 3 months notice and refund depends on finding a new tenant; consumer commission orders full refund with 9%
Article Text:
AI Image Used For Representational Purpose Only]





BENGALURU: A Bengaluru tenant who moved out of a rented flat after his office shifted to another part of the city has won a consumer court battle over his Rs 80,000 security deposit. The III Additional Bengaluru Urban District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has ordered the landlord to return the entire deposit with 9% annual interest and pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation expenses.The commission found that the landlord had failed to provide evidence of damage to the property or establish any outstanding payments that could justify withholding the money. The order was passed on September 26 by a bench comprising president Shivarama K and members Rekha Sayannavar and Suma Anilkumar.The dispute began after tenant Vireswar Mahanta decided to leave the flat following the relocation of his workplace from Nagawara to Whitefield. Mahanta had paid Rs 80,000 as a refundable security deposit and was paying monthly rent of Rs 25,000. According to the complaint, he informed landlord Basireddy Kondareddy on March 16, 2026, about his decision to vacate the property.He handed over the keys and possession on March 30, claiming that the flat had been left in good condition.However, the security deposit was not returned. Mahanta alleged that the landlord repeatedly avoided his requests and told him during a WhatsApp call on April 16 that the money would be returned only after another tenant was found for the flat.The tenant argued that the rental agreement did not require him to wait for a replacement occupant before receiving his deposit. After a legal notice sent on April 30 went unanswered, he approached the consumer commission seeking the refund, 12% annual interest, Rs 1 lakh in compensation for mental agony and financial hardship, and Rs 25,000 towards legal expenses.Kondareddy disputed the allegations, maintaining that Mahanta had not given the three months' advance notice stipulated under Clause 7 of their rental agreement. He also argued that the deposit could be used to recover outstanding rent, utility bills, maintenance charges and expenses incurred on repairs or damage to the property.The commission examined the rental agreement, payment records, WhatsApp conversations, photographs and a video recording of the flat placed on record by Mahanta. It noted that the landlord had acknowledged receiving the Rs 80,000 deposit. However, he had not produced convincing evidence of damage to the premises or provided a satisfactory account of any unpaid bills or other outstanding dues.The commission also took note of the tenant's payment records, which showed that he had paid rent for four months without default. It said a landlord could not retain the entire security deposit indefinitely merely on the ground that deductions might be necessary. The commission held that withholding the deposit without evidence to support the proposed deductions amounted to deficiency in service and an unfair trade practice.It directed Kondareddy to return Rs 80,000 with 9% annual interest, calculated from March 30, 2026, when Mahanta handed over the flat, until the amount is realised. The landlord was also ordered to pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs, taking the principal amount payable to Rs 90,000, apart from interest.He has been given 45 days to comply with the order. The commission further directed that if the landlord fails to pay within the stipulated period, the Rs 10,000 litigation cost will also attract interest at 9% per annum from September 29, 2026, until realisation.
Article Summary: Vireswar Mahanta moved out of a rented flat after his office shifted to another part of the city. He handed over the keys and possession on March 30, claiming that the flat had been left in good condition. However, the security deposit was not returned. Mahanta alleged that the landlord repeatedly avoided his requests.

Article Title: Chandigarh man books son's Winnipeg-Delhi flight tickets in 2022, cancels them 6 days before travel; consumer commission orders Yatra Online, Air Canada and Etihad Airways to refund Rs 70,878 with 9%
Article Text:
AI Image Used For Representational Purpose Only





CHANDIGARH: A Chandigarh resident who cancelled flight tickets booked for his son shortly before the scheduled journey was denied a refund despite initially being told by the booking platform that the cancellation process had been initiated.The Chandigarh District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has now directed Yatra Online, Air Canada and Etihad Airways to refund Rs 70,878 to the complainant.The complainant had booked tickets for his son to travel from Winnipeg to New Delhi on November 3, 2022. Article Title: Delhi. Can’t breathe. Can’t move; AQI inches closer to severe; share of farm fires as high as 16.2%
Article Text:
Delhi's air quality index is deteriorating and expected to reach severe levels by Friday (Photo credit: Tarun Rawat)

NCR's best and worst





NEW DELHI: Delhi’s air quality deteriorated further within very poor levels Wednesday, inching closer to the severe category. Local emission sources contributed 31% and external sources 69% to overall air pollution in the city, with the contribution of stubble burning spiking to 16.2% against 8.2% Tuesday.The air quality index (AQI), on a scale of 0 to 500, was 377 against 350 a day earlier at 4pm. The pollution monitoring agencies are anticipating the pollution levels to spike further to severe by Friday.According to IITM’s forecast, the share of pollution from stubble burning in neighbouring states has drastically increased, with Decision Support System’s models predicting the share to rise to 20% by Friday, more than the share of vehicular pollution, which so far had dominated the city’s emission inventory.Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) Wednesday issued show-cause notices over stubble burning to the district commissioners and the SSPs of five districts in Punjab – Barnala, Bathinda, Fazilka, Jalandhar and Faridkot. Officials of Gurdaspur and Kapurthala districts received notices Tuesday.The air quality is likely to be in the very poor category Thursday and in the severe category for around six days from Friday, stated Air Quality Early Warning System by IITM.Despite the GRAP-II restrictions put in place by CAQM Monday and several restrictions already being implemented by Delhi govt since Nov 1 under its new winter pollution framework, AQI in many city areas has already turned severe.Under Delhi govt’s new anti-pollution framework, private construction has been banned from Nov 1 to Jan 31, with a blanket ban between Dec 10 and Jan 20. It has also banned the entry of non-Delhi-registered BS-IV or below vehicles under GRAP-II.Among the areas that slipped into severe levels were IIT Delhi with an AQI of 455, Jahangirpuri 449, Punjabi Bagh 446, Mundka 439, Vivek Vihar 436, DTU 434, Rohini 432, Narela and Alipur 429, Sonia Vihar 427, Pusa 426, RK Puram 424, Bawana 417, Dr Karni Singh Shooting Range, Siri Fort, North Campus and Patparganj 412, and ITO 411.“While transport remains the top local polluter, the spike has been intensified by regional farm fires surging during the last few days, pushing stubble smoke’s contribution to over 8 to 11%. Trapped local emissions and weather stagnation drive this crisis, with farm fires acting as a serious add-on,” said Anumita Roychowdhury, executive director of CSE.The city saw a hazy and partly cloudy sky Wednesday, with the Met department expecting shallow fog and mist Thursday morning. The maximum temperature at base station Safdarjung was 29.8 degrees Celsius, a notch below normal, against 29.1 degrees Celsius a day earlier.The minimum temperature was 16.1 degrees Celsius, a notch above normal, against 16.4 a day earlier.Maximum and minimum temperatures are to hover between 27-29 and 14-17 degrees Celsius Thursday.
Article Summary: The air quality index (AQI), on a scale of 0 to 500, was 377 against 350 a day earlier at 4pm. Pollution monitoring agencies are anticipating the pollution levels to spike further to severe by Friday. Local emission sources contributed 31% and external sources 69% to overall air pollution in the city.

Article Title: How Hyderabad-linked call centre targeted 20 lakh Americans
Article Text:
A call centre fraud network linked to Hyderabad targeted nearly 20 lakh Americans through deceitful practices

Global Network

How the fraud operated

Cash, gold collected from victims

Crypto, hawala trail





HYDERABAD: A Hyderabad-linked call centre fraud network allegedly targeted nearly 20 lakh Americans, many of them elderly, using fake law enforcement threats and scam alerts, while an overseas collection network picked up cash and gold directly from victims’ homes, Enforcement Directorate (ED) stated.ED, which arrested four more accused Wednesday, said its probe uncovered a transnational network spanning India, the US, Dubai and Hong Kong, with proceeds allegedly routed through cryptocurrency channels, mule accounts and hawala operators before being brought into India.The investigation began with the Madhapur call centre case in Hyderabad and subsequently led to the busting of operational call centres in Chandigarh, Patiala and Pune.The scale of the operation emerged from WhatsApp groups recovered during the investigation. ED said the groups recorded 927 approved collections worth $27.39 million (Rs 261 crore) between July 2025 and Sept 2026.According to ED, fraudsters procured databases containing nearly 20 lakh telephone numbers, names, addresses and ages of US residents, many of them senior citizens.The data was fed into auto diallers hosted on servers in Germany and Finland.Preliminary findings indicated the personal information may have been sourced from the dark web and other online platforms.Forensic analysis of seized devices so far identified 549 American victims and targets who had already lost their life savings. Many were born in the 1940s.Investigators said these victims represented only a small fraction of the much larger pool of potential targets contained in the lead databases.The scam typically began with a fake purchase notification, a refund offer, or an alert about a computer virus. Victims were either persuaded to call a toll-free helpline or received calls that appeared to originate from US numbers.Inside the call centres, employees were assigned specific roles. According to ED, “diallers” made the initial contact; “bankers” assessed victims’ financial holdings, and “closers” posed as US govt officials to extract money from them.Callers impersonated officials from drug enforcement administration, department of justice, Federal Trade Commission and US Treasury.To bolster their claims, they allegedly used forged badges, identity cards, seizure notices and court orders, falsely linking victims’ bank accounts to drug trafficking or money laundering cases.To prevent arrest or freezing of their savings, victims were allegedly instructed to maintain secrecy and surrender their money for supposed govt safekeeping.The operation extended beyond telephone calls. ED said US-based associates were deployed to collect cash and gold directly from victims’ homes, while others received parcels through courier stores.Victims were allegedly instructed to purchase gold bars, conceal cash in courier packages, transfer funds to designated accounts, buy gift cards or deposit money through Bitcoin ATMs.Investigators said arrested accused Jaswant Singh coordinated cash pickups and parcel collections in the US and helped route the proceeds into channels that eventually converted them into rupees.Sleuths also recovered Social Security details of 140 Americans along with personal and banking information. ED alleged that identity documents were misused to receive parcels in other people’s names and to create front entities to receive money.Cryptocurrency was used both to move illicit proceeds and to fund the infrastructure needed to run the fraud network, ED alleged.Lead databases, internet-calling services and dialler systems were allegedly paid for using USDT.The money trail ran through US mule accounts, companies in Dubai and Hong Kong, cryptocurrency wallets, and hawala and angadia channels before reaching India.ED said the proceeds were subsequently invested in properties, gold, vehicles, and businesses.Meanwhile, ED’s Hyderabad zonal office continued tracing additional beneficiaries and identifying remaining proceeds of crime.
Article Summary: ED said its probe uncovered a transnational network spanning India, the US, Dubai and Hong Kong. Proceeds allegedly routed through cryptocurrency channels, mule accounts and hawala operators before being brought into India. ED said US- based associates were deployed to collect cash and gold directly from victims’ homes.

Article Title: Jeff Bezos gave Eva Longoria and Bill McRaven $100 million, but she challenges the belief that giving back requires wealth, saying ‘impact doesn’t come from how much money you have’
Article Text:
How Jeff Bezos brought Eva Longoria and Bill McRaven together

Why Eva Longoria believes giving back is about more than money

What Longoria has done with her philanthropic award

What Bill McRaven plans to do with his $50 million

Growing debate over billionaire philanthropy and public responsibility

Philanthropy is often associated with people who have fortunes large enough to fund schools, charities and ambitious social programmes. Yet the ability to support others does not necessarily depend on the size of a bank account. As reported by Fortune, actress Eva Longoria has been making that distinction after receiving a $50 million philanthropic award from Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sánchez Bezos, alongside retired US Navy admiral Bill McRaven. Two years after the recognition, Longoria says the experience has changed how she approaches charitable work, but she also wants to challenge the idea that meaningful contributions are reserved for wealthy individuals.In 2024, Eva Longoria and retired admiral Bill McRaven were selected as recipients of the Bezos Courage and Civility Award, an initiative established by Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos to recognise people working to improve society.“The Courage and Civility Award makes it possible for us at the Eva Longoria Foundation to create long-term impact with transformative giving.”Each recipient received $50 million, bringing the combined philanthropic commitment to $100 million.The funding was intended to support causes that reflected their respective areas of work.For Longoria, the award offered an opportunity to expand programmes focused on education, economic opportunities and support for Latino communities in the United States. McRaven, meanwhile, had plans to direct his share towards education and support services for military personnel and their families.McRaven is widely recognised for overseeing the 2011 US military operation that resulted in the death of al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden.Longoria's experience with the award has given her a larger platform to discuss charitable giving, but her message is not centred on financial donations. In an interview with Fortune, she said, “This award has allowed me to continue investing those resources into the communities and causes I care deeply about—supporting Latina entrepreneurs, expanding access to education, and backing organizations that are driving real change on the ground. ”Her understanding of giving back includes mentoring, sharing professional knowledge and helping small businesses find opportunities they might otherwise struggle to access.Longoria's involvement in charitable work began well before she received recognition from Bezos. In 2012, she established the Eva Longoria Foundation, which focuses on improving educational and entrepreneurial opportunities for Latinas in the United States. Its work includes helping women access resources that can support their education and participation in business. She also founded Eva's Heroes, an organisation that supports young adults with intellectual special needs.The $50 million award has provided additional resources for these efforts. Longoria has described the funding as an opportunity to plan longer-term programmes and direct investment towards communities and organisations working on the ground.Her charitable activities also sit alongside a varied business career. The former Desperate Housewives actress has developed interests in entertainment, entrepreneurship and sports, including her luxury tequila brand Casa Del Sol, production company Hyphenate Media Group and investment in women's football club Angel City FC.She has also been associated with an early investment in the John Wick film franchise. These business activities have helped establish her as more than an actor, while her foundation work has remained a separate part of her public life. Longoria has said,“Receiving that support was incredibly meaningful, not just because of the scale of the gift, but because it represented trust and responsibility.”The other half of the $100 million commitment went to Bill McRaven, whose philanthropic priorities reflect his military background. McRaven has said he intends to support educational programmes for future military leaders and children of deceased veterans. Mental health assistance for serving military personnel is another area included in his plans.A former four-star admiral, McRaven held senior leadership positions in the US military and later served as chancellor of the University of Texas System. His work has included military education, leadership development and public service.The Bezos Courage and Civility Award has previously recognised other prominent figures involved in humanitarian and social initiatives. Among its recipients are civil rights advocate Van Jones, chef and humanitarian José Andrés, and singer Dolly Parton.Large charitable donations attract attention because they can finance projects that would be difficult for smaller organisations to undertake. But the concentration of philanthropic resources among a relatively small number of wealthy individuals has also raised questions about how much responsibility should rest with them. The Giving Pledge is one example of an effort to encourage large-scale charitable commitments. Established in 2010 by Bill Gates, Melinda French Gates and Warren Buffett, it invites billionaires to commit at least half of their wealth to charitable causes during their lifetimes or through their wills.More than 250 individuals and families have signed the pledge since its launch. However, making a commitment and distributing the promised wealth are not the same thing. For Liz Baker, chief executive of Greater Good Charities, waiting for wealthy donors to address community problems leaves too much work undone. The organisation she leads has distributed more than $1 billion in support across 121 countries since 2006. Speaking to Fortune, Baker argued that charitable participation should not be limited to people capable of making substantial financial contributions.
Article Summary: Actress Eva Longoria received a $50 million philanthropic award from Jeff Bezos. She was given the award alongside retired US Navy admiral Bill McRaven. Longoria says the experience has changed how she approaches charitable work. She also wants to challenge the idea that meaningful contributions are reserved for wealthy individuals.

Article Title: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s tax proposal that will come for houses of Jeff Bezos, Michael Dell and other millionaires clears legal hurdle; what the court says
Article Text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s tax proposal that will come for houses of Jeff Bezos, Michael Dell and other millionaires clears legal hurdle

New York City administration sent initial notice in July

Zohran Mamdani reacts

New York City Mayor Zohran Mandani scored a legal victory after a state appeals court reversed a lower court ruling that had previously ordered his administration to redo the rollout of a tax on high-end second homes. Called the “pied-à-terre tax”, it would apply to homes worth over $5 million that are not the owner’s main residence. The ruling reverses a previous ruling by Staten Island judge dated September 29 that the city had mishandled the rollout and ordered officials to restart the process. According to a Fox News report, the four judge panel unanimously dismissed the homeowners' lawsuit stating that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing. Under the new ruling, Mamdani’s administration gets a go ahead to continue implementing the surcharge on the ultra-rich.Announced earlier this year, the tax could impact billionaires including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Dell CEO Michael Dell.In a post on X earlier this year in July, Mamdani said owners of second homes in New York City worth more than $5 million should "check your mailbox" because the city has started sending notification letters about its upcoming pied-à-terre tax."If you have a second home in New York City worth more than $5M, check your mailbox when you're back in the five boroughs — because you've got mail," Mamdani wrote in the post dated July 24."Today, we sent notification letters to property owners, letting them know that our new pied-à-terre tax is coming soon."Reacting to the latest ruling, Zohran Mamdani said: “From day one, those with the most have attempted to use every legal avenue available to shield their wealth and avoid contributing more to our city”.Randy Mastro, an attorney representing the homeowners, criticized the court for dismissing the lawsuit without addressing the merits of their challenge. "It’s a shame that, after the City admittedly botched the rollout of this surcharge, the court today took the procedural offramp of standing to avoid addressing the merits of this case," Mastro said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital."What the City has done here is unconscionable — trying to ensnare thousands of people who don’t owe this surcharge into having to prove they live in their own homes or else have to pay it. But now, this lawless and chaotic data collection scheme will go unremedied."
Article Summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani scored a legal victory after a state appeals court reversed a lower court ruling that had previously ordered his administration to redo the rollout of a tax on high-end second homes. The ruling reverses a previous ruling by Staten Island judge dated September 29 that the city had mishandled the rollout and ordered officials to restart the process.

Article Title: Priscilla Chan's letter on '2026 milestone' of 10-years of association and $100 million commitment to the island community: What began as a desire to ...
Article Text:
Priscilla Chan: ‘What began as a desire to give back'

More than 100 organisations supported

Focus on community-led solutions

Looking ahead

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan have reached a decade of philanthropy on the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi. In a letter published by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI), Chan called 2026 a meaningful milestone for her family. Since 2016, the couple has committed more than $100 million to over 100 local organisations. Chan wrote that the giving began as a wish to support a place the family calls home and has grown into lasting partnerships with groups working to strengthen communities and care for local families. She said the approach has been built on listening, with yearly conversations with residents, community leaders and service providers shaping priorities. She also thanked the community for the chance to learn, volunteer and build relationships on the island.Chan reflected on the family's 10-year association with Kauaʻi and the philanthropic efforts undertaken since 2016 in the message published by han Zuckerberg Initiative. She recalled that this journey of philanthropy started with a simple wish to offer support to a community which had become a crucial part of their lives and evolved into partnerships focused on strengthening local communities, supporting families and protecting the island's unique culture and environment."2026 marks a meaningful milestone for our family: a decade of philanthropy on Kauaʻi and more than $100 million committed to over 100 local organizations," Chan wrote. She further added that listening to the people, community leaders and service providers has helped the family in prioritising throughout the decade.As per the initiate, the philanthropic programme offered support to 101 organisations, awarded 296 grants and committed $111 million across Hawaiʻi, including more than $57 million invested directly in Kauaʻi. The organisation further mentioned that the funding has been directed towards seven key areas: health and wellbeing, affordable housing, ʻāina and culture, workforce development, education and youth, food production and distribution, and emergency relief.* Health: This is the largest area of investment, with grants to 18 local organisations. It includes a $10 million commitment to the University of Hawaiʻi medical school’s Kauaʻi Medical Training Track, which gives full scholarships to doctors who agree to practise on the island. The program has 22 future doctors in training and graduated its first five this year. Funding has also gone to a new CT scanner at Wilcox Hospital, urgent care on the North Shore, and mental health services.* Housing: Nearly a quarter of all Kauaʻi giving has gone to affordable housing. This includes $5.4 million for Kauaʻi Habitat for Humanity and $876,000 to Permanently Affordable Living Hawaiʻi to put homes into a community land trust.* Land and culture: More than 20 organisations have received support, including $4 million to preserve the Alakoko fishpond and $675,000 for the Kāhili Beach Preserve. A separate $50 million went to the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa for ocean research.* Workforce: A $4.2 million gift during the pandemic revived the county’s Rise to Work program, which created jobs for 364 unemployed residents. Many still hold those roles.* Education and youth: This area has the most recipients, over 40 organisations, including every public and public charter school on the island.* Food: Grants have supported food banks and pantries, local farming and distribution to families and elders.* Emergency relief: After Hurricane Lowell, the couple donated to the Kauaʻi Strong Fund within a day. They also committed $6 million to pandemic relief in 2020 and 2021 and contributed to Maui wildfire relief in 2023.Chan highlighted the importance of community-led philanthropy via her message. She highlighted that meaningful giving beings with listening and learning from the people who are facing challenges. The report also incorporated testimonials from multiple local organisations and also described the approach as trust-based and focused on supporting existing community efforts.Marking the 10-year milestone, Chan said her family's commitment remains unchanged. The focus, she said, will continue to be on listening to community voices, supporting local organisations and responding to the island's needs. "A decade in, the commitment remains the same: listen to community voices, support the organizations already doing the work, and respond when Kauaʻi needs it most," the report said.
Article Summary: Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan have reached a decade of philanthropy on the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi. Since 2016, the couple has committed more than $100 million to over 100 local organisations. Chan said the approach has been built on listening, with yearly conversations with residents, community leaders and service providers shaping priorities.

Article Title: Apple sends AI warning, tells it is not immune to attacks by AI Agents; they may send communication or may transactions that ...
Article Text:
Apple highlights risks from autonomous AI agents

Warning includes concerns about hidden or manipulated information

Part of a wider pattern

AI investments drive costs higher

Apple CEO John Ternus stresses user awareness and privacy

Apple has expanded its warnings about the risks of artificial intelligence, cautioning that autonomous AI agents could access systems without authorisation, send communications, execute transactions and behave in unpredictable ways that may threaten businesses and users, as reported by Fortune. The warning was included in the iPhone maker's latest annual 10-K filing, released a day after the company reported its fourth-quarter financial results. It said AI agents and similar technologies can act on their own: interacting with internal or external systems they may not be authorised to access, executing or altering code, sending communications and completing transactions. Such tools, Apple said, may behave in unintended or unpredictable ways. That includes taking actions nobody directed or authorised, exceeding permissions, or defying and resisting instructions. The company also said rogue agents could conceal their actions, withhold or manipulate information, or generate inaccurate or deceptive outputs.In the risk factors section of its annual filing, Apple said AI agents and similar technologies are capable of taking actions independently, including interacting with internal and external systems, executing or altering code, sending communications and completing transactions.The company warned that such systems may sometimes attempt to access platforms or services they are not authorised to use. Apple said these technologies could "behave in unintended or unpredictable ways," including taking actions that were not directed, instructed or authorised. The company also warned that AI systems could exceed permissions, ignore instructions or act in ways that differ from their intended purpose.The company raised concerns that rogue AI agents could conceal their activities or manipulate information. According to Apple, autonomous AI systems may "conceal actions, hide, withhold or manipulate information, or generate inaccurate or deceptive outputs."The expanded disclosure reflects growing concern across the technology industry about agentic AI systems, which are designed to work more independently and carry out complex tasks on behalf of users.Apple is not the first big tech company to flag the risk. Alphabet recently raised similar concerns in its own filing, and went further. It said it had seen unexpected behaviour during AI model testing, including agents acting outside their intended scope, which it warned could lead to “severe or catastrophic” security and societal incidents. Fortune noted that these warnings follow several major AI-related security incidents, most notably an attack on Hugging Face by OpenAI agents this summer. Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, made public last week, also lists cases where its models gained unauthorised access to real-world systems during security testing.Microsoft has announced controls to detect, monitor and restrict AI agents, including cutting their permissions or stopping them if they act suspiciously. CEO Satya Nadella has argued that companies should treat agents as potential insider risks and build security controls outside the AI model.Beyond AI safety concerns, Apple's filing also highlighted challenges related to its AI ambitions. The company said growing demand for cloud computing, storage and AI infrastructure is creating supply constraints, longer lead times and rising costs. Apple noted that shortages of memory and storage components are expected to intensify and could affect its AI rollout plans. The company added that research and development spending rose 32% year-over-year, driven in part by higher infrastructure costs and continued AI investments.Speaking after the company’s earnings announcement, CEO John Ternus explained that the agentic AI capabilities as promising tools for users but stressed that people must completely understand the access and permissions they grant such systems. Trenus also pointed out the Apple’s ocus on security and privacy as it continues developing AI-powered features and services.The warning underscores a broader shift across the technology sector as companies race to deploy increasingly capable AI agents while simultaneously acknowledging the security, privacy and operational risks that can emerge when autonomous systems gain greater access to data, software and real-world actions.
Article Summary: Apple warns that autonomous AI agents could access systems without authorisation, send communications, execute transactions and behave in unpredictable ways. The warning was included in the iPhone maker's latest annual 10-K filing, released a day after the company reported its fourth-quarter financial results. Apple also highlighted challenges related to its AI ambitions.

Article Title: Qualcomm is selling fewer phone chips, earning less on each and charging more for them
Article Text:
Qualcomm’s phone chip sales drop 26%

Qualcomm’s chip margins are shrinking despite the price hikes

Qualcomm’s biggest Android customers are shipping fewer phones

Qualcomm's smartphone chip business shrank by about a quarter in the September quarter, according to the company's latest earnings report. Handset chip revenue fell 26% to $5.14 billion from $6.96 billion a year ago, wiping out roughly $1.8 billion in sales and missing the StreetAccount estimate of $5.21 billion. Adjusted earnings per share dropped 28% to $2.17, adjusted pre-tax profit fell 30%, and total adjusted revenue slipped 7% to $10.44 billion.Its chips are about to get more expensive too. The Snapdragon maker is raising prices across its products, citing rising costs in wafer fabrication, chip packaging, memory and other materials. It already raised prices in September, and phone chip sales fell anyway. The stock slid as much as 7% in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the company’s forecast for the current quarter came in below expectations. Before the results, it was up just 1.3% for the year.The price increases are not protecting margins yet, and the company says they won’t fully do so until the second half of fiscal 2027, which begins in April. Revenue at its chip division fell 8% to $9.02 billion, and its pre-tax margin dropped to 24% from 29% a year ago. For this quarter, Qualcomm has guided for 20% to 22%. It puts three points of that fall down to folding its data centre unit, which is spending heavily ahead of its revenue ramp, into the chip segment.The full year was no better. Handset chip revenue fell 13% to $24.07 billion in fiscal 2026, about $3.7 billion less than the year before. Adjusted earnings per share dropped 12% to $10.54, and adjusted pre-tax profit fell 16%. The company still spent $7.8 billion buying back its own shares over the year.Licensing, the business that collects royalties from phone makers using the company’s patents, slipped as well. Its revenue fell 7% to $1.3 billion in the quarter, and its profit dropped 10%, even after it renewed licensing deals with Apple, Huawei and Transsion.The forecast offers little comfort. Qualcomm expects adjusted earnings of $2.15 to $2.35 a share this quarter, a midpoint below the $2.27 analysts had pencilled in. It also expects the smartphone market, which still drives most of its chip sales, to stay flat through 2027.The slide in handset revenue mirrors the trouble at the phone makers Qualcomm sells to. Rising memory prices have forced brands to raise prices and cut production. Global smartphone shipments fell 20% year-on-year in the July to September quarter, according to Counterpoint Research. OPPO and Vivo, two of the chipmaker’s major Android customers, each shipped more than 20% fewer phones than a year ago.Xiaomi, another key customer, also cut shipments. It is now using its own XRING O3 chipset to set its premium phones apart, the same segment where Qualcomm sells its most expensive chips.The data centre business Qualcomm wants investors to focus on is being held back as well. CEO Cristiano Amon said the unit is limited by supply. “If I had more supply, I would probably be doing better,” he said.Qualcomm is now asking phone makers to pay more for its chips at a time when they are already struggling to sell phones. By the company’s own timeline, the higher prices won’t fully show up in its margins until April at the earliest.
Article Summary: Handset chip revenue fell 26% to $5.14 billion from $6.96 billion a year ago. Qualcomm is raising prices across its products, citing rising costs in wafer fabrication, chip packaging, memory and other materials. It already raised prices in September, and phone chip sales fell anyway.

Article Title: Jeff Bezos' ex-wife MacKenzie Scott who sold half of her Amazon stake, gave $30 million to a nonprofit community loan fund in Silicon Valley in 2024, a year later it shared 10-year plan to transform B
Article Text:
From MacKenzie Scott’s surprise donation to long-term strategy

The 10-year plan

Building on 25 years of housing investment

A year after Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife MacKenzie Scott gave $30 million to a Silicon Valley-based nonprofit community loan fund Housing Trust Silicon Valley has unveiled a 10-year strategy aimed at turning the one-time gift into lasting housing solutions across the Bay Area. The organisation says the funding will help expand affordable housing initiatives, support first-time homebuyers, strengthen policy advocacy efforts and back innovative housing projects over the next decade. a San Jose-based community loan fund, announced on September 30, 2025, a 10-year plan for turning the unrestricted gift from Scott’s Yield Giving fund into long-term housing solutions across the Bay Area.Housing Trust announced the donation on October 2, 2024. CEO Noni Ramos called it “the largest from an individual in our history” and said it came as a surprise. The gift was unrestricted, which means the nonprofit can decide how to use it, and it was meant to help the organisation expand its work across the 14-county greater Bay Area. At the time, early ideas for the money included seeding a new capital raise for its loan fund, expanding existing programmes and launching new initiatives to deepen partnerships and increase equity and affordability in housing.The release highlighted two recent projects as examples of its work. At Meridian Apartments in Sunnyvale, Housing Trust provided a $2 million predevelopment loan, in partnership with Related California, to help create 90 affordable homes for families. In San Rafael, it supported Eden Housing with a $4 million loan for Vivalon, a 66-unit development for older adults that pairs affordable homes with supportive services.The plan, developed with input from staff, the board and community stakeholders, has five major initiatives:* Lending capital and new products: Expanding the core revolving loan fund and piloting new tools to meet developers’ changing needs. More details were due at the organisation’s Investor Briefing on October 15.* Homeownership expansion: Beginning in 2026, extending first-time homebuyer programmes to reach more households across a wider area.* Policy and partnerships: Hiring new staff to strengthen advocacy and collaboration across sectors that could unlock more resources and affordable housing.* Impact measurement and management: Launching a framework in early 2026 to better track, evaluate and communicate results.* Innovation investments: Supporting mission-driven housing innovations that can reduce costs, shorten development timelines and increase affordability.Noni Ramos CEO of Housing Trust said the gift allows the organisation to take bold steps and carries both the responsibility and the freedom to scale what works, take calculated risks on new ideas and widen its reach. Board Chair Lisa Gutierrez, a senior vice president at U.S. Bank, said the plan is not about one-time dollars but about building momentum that compounds. By putting the funds to work strategically, she said, Housing Trust can attract new partners, expand homeownership and make loans to create and preserve rental housing in ways it could not before, while also strengthening the organisation itself.The announcement comes as Housing Trust Silicon Valley marks its 25th anniversary. Since its founding in 2000, the community development financial institution says it has invested more than $690 million, helped create over 28,700 affordable housing opportunities and supported more than 53,800 residents in finding homes they can afford. The organisation says its work has also leveraged nearly $9 billion in additional public and private capital.Board Chair Lisa Gutierrez said the goal is to use the donation strategically to attract new partners, expand homeownership opportunities and support loans for creating and preserving affordable rental housing, while strengthening the organisation's long-term capacity.The nonprofit said the decade-long strategy is designed to ensure that MacKenzie Scott's donation continues generating impact long after the original gift was received, helping create more affordable and stable housing opportunities across the Bay Area.
Article Summary: Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife MacKenzie Scott gave $30 million to a Silicon Valley-based nonprofit community loan fund Housing Trust Silicon Valley. The organisation says the funding will help expand affordable housing initiatives, support first- time homebuyers, strengthen policy advocacy efforts and back innovative housing projects.

Article Title: Trump's midterm setback may ease tariff pressure on India: Report
Article Text: US President Donald Trump's electoral setback in the 2026 midterm elections could ease trade-related pressure on India and give New Delhi greater room to negotiate favourable terms in its ongoing trade talks with Washington.According to a research report by Emkay Research, the Democrats' victory and the loss of Republican control over both chambers of Congress could limit Trump's ability to pursue an aggressive tariff agenda. The changed political equation could reduce the threat of fresh tariff escalation and weaken Washington's leverage over its trading partners, including India."The midterms outcome probably will not change the tariff structure much, but it will change Trump's incentives: fewer new escalation tools, more pressure to deliver consumer affordability, and deals before 2028," the report said.The report noted that the urgency for India to conclude a trade agreement with the US has diminished following the election outcome. It suggested that New Delhi could now negotiate from a stronger position rather than face pressure to quickly accept Washington's trade demands."Trade remains one of the few areas he (Trump) controls alone, however, so headline volatility will persist even as the bias softens," it added.Emkay Research also highlighted that the US Supreme Court's ruling on Trump's use of emergency economic powers had limited one route for imposing tariffs. It said future tariff escalation would increasingly require investigation-based action under Section 301 and Section 232 of US trade law.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump's electoral setback in the 2026 midterm elections could ease trade-related pressure on India. New Delhi could now negotiate from a stronger position rather than face pressure to quickly accept Washington's trade demands. The urgency for India to conclude a trade agreement with the US has diminished following the election outcome.
